title: Modern cosmology
one_line_summary: Rewrites Friedmann's equation in terms of present-day density parameters, maps every FRW model onto the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane with a particle-in-a-potential analysis, then shows how H0, the CMB, nucleosynthesis, rotation curves, supernovae and CMB anisotropies locate our universe at the flat ΛCDM point, before running the clock back through the thermal history, motivating inflation, discussing anthropic arguments and closing the book with the open questions of cosmology.
role_in_book: Last chapter of Part F and of the whole book, written largely for the second edition. Chapter 24 set up the Robertson-Walker geometry, Friedmann's equations, redshift, the book's luminosity distance and the deceleration parameter; Chapter 25 solved single-component dust and radiation models and studied horizons and conformal structure. This chapter changes viewpoint from 'solve for R(t) given C, Λ, k' to the observational cosmologist's language of Ω parameters, so that theory can be confronted with data and the concordance ΛCDM model identified. From §26.3 on it deliberately imports physics outside general relativity (black-body radiation, atomic and nuclear energy scales, particle dark matter candidates, scalar fields), flagged as Level 2 and to be taken partly on trust. Its closing section ties cosmology back to the horizons and singularities of Part D, the gravitational-wave detectors of Part E, and the book-long aim of preparing readers for Hawking and Ellis.

learning_objectives: Reader can define the critical density and the density parameters Ωr, Ωm, ΩΛ and Ωc, and explain why they sum to exactly one at the present epoch.

Reader can rewrite the multi-component Friedmann equation in the dimensionless variables R̃ = R/R0 and t̃ = H0 t and interpret it as motion of a unit mass in the effective potential V(R̃) with energy E = Ωc/2.
Reader can derive the dividing lines of the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane: closed/open along ΩΛ = 1 − Ωm, accelerating/decelerating along ΩΛ = Ωm/2, and the big-bang/bounce boundary from V_max = E.
Reader can express the age of an FRW universe as an integral over R̃ and evaluate it for a flat matter-plus-Λ model, getting H0 t0 ≈ 0.96 for Ωm = 0.3.
Reader can explain why H0 must be measured with distant objects and how peculiar velocities, standard candles and the calibration problem lead to a cosmic distance ladder.
Reader can obtain ε = αT⁴ from the Planck spectrum, turn the CMB temperature into Ωr ≈ 10⁻⁴, and show that T ∝ 1/R keeps a black-body spectrum thermal as the universe expands.
Reader can make the crude decoupling estimate from the hydrogen ionization energy and explain the two reasons the real decoupling temperature (≈3000 K) is about ten times lower.

Reader can list the independent routes to Ωm (star counts, nucleosynthesis, rotation curves, supernova redshift-magnitude data, CMB anisotropies) and explain how crossing SN and CMB constraints give Ωm ≈ 0.3, ΩΛ ≈ 0.7 and a flat universe.
Reader can derive the exact luminosity distance-redshift relation for matter plus Λ, with its sin, linear and sinh forms for k = +1, 0, −1.
Reader can place matter-radiation equality, decoupling, nucleosynthesis-era temperatures and the quark-hadron transition in time using T ∝ 1/R with R ∝ t^{2/3} or t^{1/2}.

Reader can state the flatness problem (|1 − Ω| ∝ t^{2/3} in the matter era) and the horizon problem (particle horizon 2t in the radiation era) quantitatively and show how exponential expansion removes both.
Reader can derive φ̈ + 3Hφ̇ + V'(φ) = 0 and the scalar-field energy-momentum tensor, and explain why slow roll makes T_ab ≈ V g_ab act like a cosmological constant.
Reader can distinguish the book's weak and strong anthropic principles and summarize the objections raised against the strong form.

Reader can list the unresolved questions behind ΛCDM: the nature of dark matter, the origin of dark energy and the vacuum-energy mismatch, the physics of the inflaton, the averaging problem, and the status of the initial singularity.

teaching_approach.summary: A survey chapter that starts with explicit, calculus-level manipulation and progressively hands over to physics the reader is asked to accept on trust. Section 26.1 is the mathematical core: Friedmann's equation is made dimensionless, reinterpreted as a particle moving in a potential, and used with elementary calculus on V(R̃) to carve the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane into regions of qualitatively different universes. Each later section supplies one number or one constraint for that plane: H0 from distance ladders, Ωr from the CMB temperature, baryons from nucleosynthesis, dark matter from rotation curves, and the crossing supernova and CMB strips that single out ΛCDM. The authors then run the model backwards with two scaling laws and order-of-magnitude arithmetic, introduce inflation as a cure computed from the very formulas that expose the flatness and horizon problems, and finish in a discursive, partly philosophical register (anthropic principles, arrows of time, Wheeler's U) with an honest list of what is still unexplained.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: Chapter 25 treated radiation, matter and vacuum one at a time; how do we handle a universe containing all three, in terms that observations can pin down?
Model: define the critical density and Ω's, treat Λ as a fluid with p = −ρ, write the Friedmann equation in R̃ and t̃, and derive the sum rule Ωr + Ωm + ΩΛ + Ωc = 1.
Reinterpret as a unit mass in a potential; conclude that four numbers fix the model and, neglecting Ωr, that the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane classifies all models.
Formalism: derive the dividing lines (closed/open, accelerating, big bang or bounce, recollapse) and the age integral.
Measurement I: H0 via standard candles and distance ladders; the CMB as a black body giving Ωr and T ∝ 1/R; decoupling and the last scattering surface.
Measurement II: mass census (stars, nucleosynthesis, rotation curves), then the exact d_L(z) relation and CMB anisotropies, whose nearly perpendicular constraints fix Ωm ≈ 0.3, ΩΛ ≈ 0.7.
Application: the ΛCDM model, its exact sinh^{2/3} solution and age, and an audit of its poorly understood ingredients and of dissenting views.
Check by extrapolation: run the model backwards to matter-radiation equality, decoupling and the first second, summarized in a table of epochs.
New puzzles and a resolution: quantify the flatness and horizon problems; show exponential expansion removes both; realize it with a slowly rolling scalar field that also seeds perturbations.

Wider frame and farewell: anthropic reasoning as an alternative explanation, arrows of time, open questions about fundamental physics, and links back to singularities, horizons, gravitational waves and Hawking-Ellis.
signature_moves: Non-dimensionalizes before analysing (R̃ = R/R0, t̃ = H0 t, densities over ρcrit) so that H0 drops out as a pure scale and the Ω's are the only shape parameters.
Reuses the energy-equation idea from Chapter 25 with an explicit potential V(R̃) = −½(Ωm/R̃ + Ωr/R̃² + ΩΛR̃²) and E = Ωc/2, then turns the condition V_max = E into a curve in parameter space.
Builds one master diagram (the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane) from theory, and later overlays observational confidence regions on identical axes so that data and theory share a picture.
Crude estimate followed by a diagnosis of its failure: the decoupling temperature from mean photon energy is ten times too high, and the two physical corrections are named.
Chains simple scaling laws (T ∝ 1/R, R ∝ t^{2/3} or t^{1/2}) with a few anchor numbers to produce a thermal history without solving the full equations.
Evaluates the same particle-horizon integral for R ∝ t^{1/2} and for R ∝ e^{Ht}, so the contrast between linear and exponential growth carries the whole horizon-problem argument.
Reads the homogeneous scalar-field equation as a ball rolling in V(φ) with Hubble friction, echoing the particle-in-a-potential picture of §26.1.
Explicitly flags non-GR material as Level 2 and repeatedly names the limits of the standard model (unknown dark matter, dark energy mismatch, SN evolution, averaging, inflaton physics).

sections.title: Multi-component models
sections.summary: Starts from the Λ = 0 Friedmann equation to define the critical density 3H0²/8π (of order 10⁻²⁶ kg m⁻³) and the density parameter Ω, whose size relative to 1 fixes the sign of k. Treats Λ as a constant-density fluid with p = −ρ and writes the Friedmann equation with radiation, matter and vacuum densities scaling as R⁻⁴, R⁻³ and R⁰, then non-dimensionalizes with R̃ and t̃. Evaluating at t0 gives Ωr + Ωm + ΩΛ + Ωc = 1. The equation becomes energy conservation for a particle in V(R̃), so four parameters determine the model and H0 only sets the scale. With Ωr neglected, the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane is divided into closed/open, accelerating/decelerating and big bang/no big bang regions (the last via V_max = E and a cubic), giving Fig. 26.2. Ends with the general age integral and its closed form for flat matter-plus-Λ models.
concepts: vacuum energy as a perfect fluid
scaling of densities with the scale factor
effective potential for the scale factor
key_moves: Set k = 0 in H² = 8πρ/3 − k/R² to define ρcrit and compare the actual density with it to decide open/flat/closed.
Move Λg_ab to the source side: ρΛ = Λ/8π with p = −ρ, constant in time.
Express ρm, ρr, ρΛ as ρcrit Ω R̃⁻³, ρcrit Ω R̃⁻⁴, ρcrit ΩΛ and rescale time by the Hubble time.
Evaluate the dimensionless equation at R̃ = 1 (where dR̃/dt̃ = 1) to get the sum rule and hence Ωc from measurable Ω's.
Recast as ½(dR̃/dt̃)² + V(R̃) = E; integrate by quadrature; rescale by R0 = 1/(H0|Ωc|^{1/2}).
Neglect Ωr (≈10⁻⁴) and analyse three questions: sign of Ωc, sign of q0 = Ωm/2 − ΩΛ, and whether the potential barrier V_max exceeds E.
Maximize V at R̃³ = Ωm/2ΩΛ, impose V_max = E, cube to a cubic in ΩΛ and identify the physical roots through (0,1) and (1,0).
Separate variables once more to write H0 t0 as a definite integral from R̃ = 0 to 1.

sections.title: Measuring the Hubble constant
sections.summary: Quotes H0 = 72 ± 8 km/s/Mpc and its h-parameterization, introduces parsecs and megaparsecs with a table of cosmic distance scales, and explains why the Hubble relation z ≈ H0 d is hard to exploit: nearby galaxies are dominated by peculiar velocities, distant ones are beyond parallax and need luminosity distances. Those require standard candles (main-sequence stars, Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) whose absolute brightness must be calibrated, which astronomers do by overlapping methods forming a distance ladder.
key_moves: State H0 with its uncertainty and introduce h to carry that uncertainty through formulas.
Give distance units and a table spanning the Sun to the edge of the observable universe.
Identify the tension: nearby objects have measurable distances but large peculiar velocities; distant objects have clean Hubble flow but no direct distances.
Resolve with luminosity distances from standard candles, then name the calibration problem and the ladder solution.

sections.title: The cosmic microwave background radiation
sections.summary: Announces that much of the rest of the chapter uses physics beyond GR (marked Level 2). Recounts the prediction and discovery of the CMB and quotes T0 = 2.725 K with isotropy better than one part in 10⁴. From the Planck spectrum it extracts the peak and mean photon energies and ε = αT⁴, giving ΩCMB ≈ 5×10⁻⁵ and Ωr ≲ 10⁻⁴. Combining ε ∝ T⁴ with ρr ∝ R⁻⁴ yields T ∝ 1/R, and a black-body spectrum stays black-body because ν/T is unchanged. A hydrogen-plus-photons model gives a crude decoupling temperature of 50,000 K, corrected to about 3000 K (R̃ ≈ 10⁻³) by the spectral tail and the photon excess. Defines the observer-centred last scattering surface (radius of order 6000 Mpc), follows the photon frequency from 1.6×10¹⁴ Hz down to 160 GHz, and contrasts the black-body success with the steady-state prediction.
concepts: preservation of the black-body form under expansion
key_moves: Flag Level 2 content and say which results matter most: the scaling laws (26.36) and (26.38).
Differentiate the Planck spectrum to locate its peak; quote the mean photon energy ≈ 3k_BT.
Integrate the spectrum to get αT⁴, insert T0, convert to mass density and divide by ρcrit.
Equate ε ∝ T⁴ with ρr ∝ R⁻⁴ to obtain T ∝ 1/R; check that the thermal form is invariant because ν and T redshift together.
Estimate decoupling by 3k_BT = 14 eV, then correct for the high-energy tail and for the many photons per hydrogen atom.
Interpret the CMB as coming from a sphere around each observer, not a special place, and track its frequency redshift by ~1000.

sections.title: How heavy is the universe?
sections.summary: Builds up Ωm in stages: luminous stars give about 0.01; light-element nucleosynthesis fixes baryons at about 0.04; flat galactic rotation curves, analysed with Newtonian circular orbits v = √(GM(r)/r), reveal dark halos and motivate cold dark matter. The decisive evidence comes from two elongated constraints in the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane: the exact luminosity distance-redshift relation for Type Ia supernovae, derived from the dimensionless Friedmann equation for k = +1, 0, −1, and the multipole spectrum of CMB anisotropies, whose peak positions depend on geometry and content. The two strips cross almost at right angles near Ωm ≈ 0.3, ΩΛ ≈ 0.7, implying Ωc ≈ 0: the ΛCDM model.
concepts: CMB anisotropies and angular power spectrum
key_moves: Show star counts undercount matter (hot X-ray gas in clusters) and nucleosynthesis gives the baryon total.
Balance gravity against centripetal acceleration to predict v ∝ r^{−1/2}; flat observed curves imply unseen mass.
Replace the approximate Hubble law by an exact d_L(z): χ = ∫dt/R rewritten as an integral over R̃ with the potential inside the square root.
Describe the CMB temperature correlation C(θ) and its multipole decomposition qualitatively.
Overlay SN and CMB constraints on the model plane; their near-orthogonality gives a sharp intersection.

sections.title: The ΛCDM model of cosmology
sections.summary: Lists the model's successes (expansion history, CMB, large-scale structure, light-element abundances) and writes its exact matter-plus-Λ solution as R ∝ sinh^{2/3}(t/tΛ), which grows like t^{2/3}, decelerates, then accelerates towards de Sitter expansion; the age comes out near 14 billion years, easing tension with the oldest objects. It then audits the model: near-flatness needs explaining (inflation), roughly nine-tenths of the matter is non-baryonic, and 70% of the content is dark energy. Dark matter candidates (primordial black holes, MACHOs, massive neutrinos, axions, WIMPs) and dark energy interpretations (a constant like G, vacuum zero-point energy with a gigantic theoretical mismatch, quintessence, modified gravity) are surveyed, together with doubts about SN Ia luminosity evolution and about averaging the non-linear Einstein equations.
key_moves: Recast the Chapter 25 solution (25.5) in Ω language (Exercise 26.10) and read off early t^{2/3} and late e^{H0√ΩΛ t} behaviour.
Evaluate the age formula (26.30) for the concordance parameters.
Convert the three unexplained ingredients (flatness, dark matter, dark energy) into explicit questions.
Eliminate astrophysical dark matter candidates using the nucleosynthesis bound and lensing searches; list particle candidates.
Contrast geometric and source-side readings of Λ and quote the vacuum-energy discrepancy.
Record observational and theoretical objections to the need for Λ.

sections.title: The early Universe
sections.summary: Radiation, negligible today, dominates early because ρr/ρm = (Ωr/Ωm)/R̃. With Ωr = 7×10⁻⁵ and Ωm = 0.3 equality occurs at R̃ ≈ 2×10⁻⁴. Combining T ∝ 1/R̃ with R ∝ t^{2/3} after equality dates decoupling to about 10¹³ s and equality to about 10¹² s; switching to R ∝ t^{1/2} before equality gives T ≈ 1.5×10¹⁰ K/√t, so at one second thermal energies are about 1 MeV (nuclear scale) and the quark-hadron transition is near 10⁻⁴ s. Table 26.2 and Fig. 26.6 summarize the epochs.
concepts: scaling of densities with the scale factor
temperature-time relation in the radiation era
key_moves: Take the ratio of the radiation and matter scaling laws to locate equality in R̃.
Use two scaling laws together, T/T0 = (t0/t)^{2/3}, to convert temperatures into times after equality.
Change the exponent to 1/2 before equality and renormalize at t_eq, T_eq.
Translate temperatures into energies with E = k_BT to identify which particles are free at each epoch.

sections.title: Inflationary cosmology
sections.summary: Introduces a time-dependent critical density and shows |1 − ρ/ρcrit(t)| = |k|/(HR)² grows as t^{2/3} in the matter era, so present near-flatness implies extreme early tuning (flatness problem). Computes the particle horizon Δr = R(t)∫dt/R, equal to 2t for radiation domination, and argues that CMB photons from opposite directions left causally disconnected points (horizon problem; connected patches span only about 2°). Exponential expansion R ∝ e^{Ht} makes the horizon grow exponentially and drives |1 − Ω| to zero as e^{−2Ht}, curing both. A scalar inflaton with action (26.64) obeys φ̈ + 3Hφ̇ + V' = 0; on a flat stretch of potential Hubble damping freezes φ, so T_ab ≈ V(φ*)g_ab behaves like a cosmological constant and gives de Sitter expansion until φ rolls to the minimum. Quantum fluctuations δφ produce δρ ≈ V'δφ, which are inflated into CMB anisotropies and the seeds of structure.
key_moves: Divide the Friedmann equation by H² to isolate |1 − Ω| = |k|/(HR)² and insert R ∝ t^{2/3}, H ∝ 1/t.
Extrapolate today's 30% bound back to equality and the quark-hadron epoch.
Set ds² = 0 on a radial ray, integrate dr = dt/R and multiply by R(t) to get the proper horizon distance; evaluate for R ∝ t^{1/2}.
Use past light cones of two antipodal last-scattering points to state the horizon problem.
Re-evaluate both formulas for R ∝ e^{Ht}: horizon (e^{Ht} − 1)/H, flatness deviation ∝ e^{−2Ht}.
Vary the scalar-field action to get the field equation and T_ab; specialize to RW; argue slow roll from the damping term.
Identify T_ab ≈ V g_ab with a cosmological constant and borrow the de Sitter solution; add fluctuations δρ ≈ V'δφ.

sections.title: The anthropic principle
sections.summary: Presents anthropic reasoning (our existence constrains what we can observe) as a rival style of explanation for cosmic smoothness. The weak form confines life to suitable regions and is used to account for the universe's great age via the slow chain of galaxy formation, stellar nucleosynthesis, planet formation and evolution. Quantum cosmology and the Everett-Wheeler many-worlds picture motivate the strong form, where only a few of many universes permit life and fine-tuned constants are read as selection rather than design. Objections: unobservable universes can be ignored, accessible regions reduce the strong form to the weak one, and it reverses the Copernican lesson of the cosmological principle. Inflation plus the weak form may explain present appearances; arrows of time are mentioned; the section ends with Wheeler's 'big U' and a callback to Lillian Lieber's book from Chapter 1.
key_moves: State the general principle, then the weak and strong versions in highlighted panels.
Give the age-of-the-universe argument as the weak version's showcase.
Link the strong version to many-worlds quantum mechanics and to fine-tuned constants.
Raise three objections and settle on inflation plus the weak form.

sections.title: Final questions
sections.summary: Summarizes inflation plus ΛCDM as a precise fit to data, mentions structure formation by gravitational instability (simulations require dark matter), and lists the questions that remain: what the inflaton is and why its potential suits inflation, what dark matter is, and why there is dark energy, with possible input from string theory, conformal cyclic cosmology, accelerators and space gravitational-wave detectors. Recaps cosmic history from singularity through inflation and radiation, matter and Λ eras towards de Sitter, links horizons and singularities to Part D, cites the singularity theorems against a bounce, stresses that the big bang is in principle observable, heralds multi-messenger astronomy and LISA, and closes the book by recommending Hawking and Ellis as the next step.
key_moves: Convert cosmological successes into questions for fundamental physics.
Give the full ΛCDM + inflation timeline in one paragraph.
Argue from the singularity theorems that the initial singularity is generic, not an artefact of symmetry.
Point to observation (multi-messenger, LISA) as the arbiter and to Hawking-Ellis as the reader's next destination.

sections.title: Exercises and further reading
sections.summary: Twelve exercises keyed to §§26.1-26.7: completing the derivations marked '(exercise)' in the text, two numerical estimates (critical density, temperature at one second), the Planck integral, the ΛCDM sinh solution and a three-part scalar-field calculation. The reading list names Liddle (2004) as the chapter's main source, points to Weinberg and Hartle, to review articles on redshift surveys, the CMB and dark matter/energy, to the Eames film 'Powers of 10', and to books by Penrose, Hawking, Barrow and Tipler for the closing discussion.
concepts: vacuum energy as a perfect fluid
key_moves: Exercises mostly fill in algebra skipped in §26.1 and §26.7.
Numerical exercises anchor ρcrit and T(1 s) in SI units.

concepts.name: critical density
concepts.definition: The density that makes the spatial sections of a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker model exactly flat for a given expansion rate, ρ = 3H²/8π in geometric units (3H²/8πG in SI). The book reserves the name for today's value 3H0²/8π, of order 10⁻²⁶ kg m⁻³, and in §26.7 reintroduces the time-dependent version ρcrit(t) = 3H(t)²/8π.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the Λ = 0 Friedmann equation H² = 8πρ/3 − k/R² by asking which density kills the curvature term; frozen at t0 to give one number, then compared with the actual density to decide k.
concepts.notes: Exercise 26.2 turns 1/H0 ≈ 10¹⁰ yr into about 1.8×10⁻²⁶ kg m⁻³ (my evaluation). For H0 = 72 km/s/Mpc it is 9.7×10⁻²⁷ kg m⁻³.

concepts.name: density parameter
concepts.definition: Present mean density divided by the critical density, Ω = 8πρ(t0)/3H0². When Λ = 0, Ω > 1, Ω = 1 and Ω < 1 correspond to k = +1, 0 and −1.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced immediately after ρcrit as the standard bookkeeping device of cosmology, then split into components once Λ is included.

concepts.name: component density parameters
concepts.definition: Present densities of radiation, matter and vacuum energy, each divided by ρcrit: Ωr = ρr(t0)/ρcrit, Ωm = ρm(t0)/ρcrit, ΩΛ = ρΛ/ρcrit = Λ/3H0². Together with H0 they specify an FRW model; observed values are roughly Ωr ≈ 10⁻⁴, Ωm ≈ 0.3, ΩΛ ≈ 0.7.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined to make the densities in the multi-component Friedmann equation dimensionless; afterwards they serve as coordinates of the model plane and as the targets of observation.
prerequisites: scaling of densities with the scale factor
vacuum energy as a perfect fluid

concepts.name: curvature density parameter
concepts.definition: Ωc = −k/(H0²R0²): the curvature term of the Friedmann equation written as if it were a density fraction. It is positive for open (k = −1), zero for flat and negative for closed (k = +1) models, and equals twice the 'energy' E of the particle analogy.
concepts.how_introduced: Named so that evaluating the dimensionless Friedmann equation at the present epoch produces a sum rule, making curvature measurable from the contents.
concepts.notes: Sign convention matches the modern Ω_k.

concepts.name: cosmic sum rule
concepts.definition: At the present epoch the density parameters of all components plus the curvature parameter add to exactly one, so the spatial curvature follows from the contents: Ωc = 1 − (Ωr + Ωm + ΩΛ).
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by setting t = t0 in the dimensionless Friedmann equation, where R̃ = 1 and dR̃/dt̃ = Ṙ/(R0H0) = 1 (Exercise 26.5).

concepts.name: vacuum energy as a perfect fluid
concepts.definition: Moving Λg_ab to the source side of Einstein's equations makes the cosmological constant equivalent to a perfect fluid of constant density ρΛ = Λ/8π and pressure p = −ρΛ. Such a fluid does not dilute as space expands.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off by matching the Λ terms of Friedmann's equations (24.52)-(24.53) against density and pressure (Exercise 26.3). Reused in §26.5 to interpret dark energy as quantum zero-point energy and in §26.7 for the slow-roll stress tensor.

concepts.name: multi-component Friedmann equation
aliases: Friedmann equation with radiation, matter and Λ
concepts.definition: Ṙ²/R² = (8π/3)(ρr + ρm + ρΛ) − k/R²: the squared expansion rate is fixed by the total density of all components together with the spatial curvature term.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by rewriting (24.52) with the Λ term absorbed as a fluid; generalizes the one-component treatments of Chapter 25.
prerequisites: vacuum energy as a perfect fluid

concepts.name: scaling of densities with the scale factor
concepts.definition: In an expanding FRW universe pressure-free matter dilutes as R⁻³, radiation as R⁻⁴ (dilution plus redshift of each quantum) and vacuum energy stays constant. Hence radiation dominates at early times, matter at intermediate times and Λ at late times, with ρr/ρm ∝ 1/R.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted from energy conservation in Chapter 25 to express each density as ρcrit Ω R̃⁻ⁿ; used again in §26.3 to derive T ∝ 1/R and in §26.6 to locate matter-radiation equality.

concepts.name: dimensionless Friedmann equation
concepts.definition: Friedmann's equation in R̃ = R/R0 and t̃ = H0 t: (dR̃/dt̃)² = Ωm/R̃ + Ωr/R̃² + ΩΛR̃² + Ωc. The Ω's alone fix the shape of R̃(t̃); H0 and, for k ≠ 0, R0 only rescale time and length.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by wanting to compare the sizes of the terms: the scale factor is measured against its present value, time in Hubble times, and densities against ρcrit.

concepts.name: Hubble time
concepts.definition: The reciprocal of the Hubble constant, the natural expansion timescale; about 13.6 Gyr for H0 = 72 km/s/Mpc. Cosmic ages are naturally quoted as multiples of it (H0t0).
concepts.how_introduced: Used to define the dimensionless time t̃ = t/t_H; defined earlier in Chapter 24.

concepts.name: effective potential for the scale factor
concepts.definition: Writing the dimensionless Friedmann equation as ½(dR̃/dt̃)² + V(R̃) = E with V = −½(Ωm/R̃ + Ωr/R̃² + ΩΛR̃²) and E = Ωc/2 turns cosmic expansion into one-dimensional motion of a unit mass. Where V > E the motion is forbidden; where V = E the expansion rate vanishes (a turning point).
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as an aid for analysing (26.13); used to decide which models start from R = 0, to derive the no-big-bang boundary, and inside the square root of the exact luminosity-distance integral.
concepts.notes: E is bookkeeping, not a physical energy; the analogy reappears in §26.7 for the inflaton.

concepts.name: four-parameter specification of FRW models
aliases: cosmological parameters Ωr, Ωm, ΩΛ, H0
concepts.definition: A homogeneous isotropic model containing radiation, matter and a cosmological constant is completely fixed by Ωr, Ωm, ΩΛ and H0: E follows from the sum rule, R̃(t̃) from a quadrature, and the physical R(t) = R0 R̃(H0 t) with R0 = 1/(H0|Ωc|^{1/2}) when k ≠ 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in a highlighted panel after the quadrature and rescaling; justifies reducing cosmology to measuring four numbers, and, with Ωr small, to a plane.

concepts.name: (Ωm, ΩΛ) classification plane
concepts.definition: With radiation neglected, each point (Ωm, ΩΛ) is an FRW model. Curves divide the plane: ΩΛ = 1 − Ωm (closed above, open below), ΩΛ = Ωm/2 (accelerating above), and curves from V_max = E separating models that begin with a big bang from bouncing ones and models that expand forever from ones that recollapse.
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled from the potential analysis in §26.1 and presented as one of the most important diagrams in cosmology because its axes are measurable; §26.4 overlays supernova and CMB confidence regions on it.
prerequisites: effective potential for the scale factor

concepts.name: open, flat and closed universes
concepts.definition: Spatial sections of negative, zero or positive constant curvature. In Ω language a model is closed if Ωr + Ωm + ΩΛ > 1, flat if the sum is exactly 1 and open if it is less. With Λ ≠ 0, geometry no longer decides whether the universe recollapses.
concepts.how_introduced: First via ρ0 versus ρcrit (26.3), then generalized with Λ to the line ΩΛ = 1 − Ωm in the model plane.

concepts.name: deceleration parameter
concepts.definition: q = −RR̈/Ṙ², positive when expansion slows and negative when it speeds up. For matter plus Λ at the present epoch q0 = Ωm/2 − ΩΛ, so the model accelerates above the line ΩΛ = Ωm/2; for (0.3, 0.7), q0 = −0.55.
concepts.how_introduced: Takes (24.79) and substitutes ρm(t0) = Ωmρcrit and Λ = 8πρΛ.

concepts.name: big bang versus bounce criterion
concepts.definition: For Ωm + ΩΛ > 1 (E < 0) and ΩΛ > 0 the potential has a maximum V_max = −(3/4)(2Ωm²ΩΛ)^{1/3} at R̃³ = Ωm/2ΩΛ. If V_max < E the solution climbs over the barrier from R = 0 (a big bang). If V_max > E there are two turning points: either expansion from R = 0 to a maximum and recollapse, or contraction from large R to a minimum and re-expansion with no big bang. The condition V_max = E defines boundary curves in the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane.
concepts.how_introduced: Differentiate V, substitute the stationary point, equate to E and cube to a cubic in ΩΛ with three real roots; the root through (0, 1) bounds the no-big-bang region, the root through (1, 0) separates eternal expansion from recollapse, and the third is unphysical.
prerequisites: effective potential for the scale factor
concepts.notes: The argument that E ≥ 0 rules out turning points assumes ΩΛ ≥ 0; with ΩΛ < 0 the potential rises at large R̃ and every model recollapses.

concepts.name: age of the universe
concepts.definition: Cosmic time elapsed since R = 0: H0t0 = ∫₀¹ dR̃ [ΩrR̃⁻² + ΩmR̃⁻¹ + ΩΛR̃² + Ωc]^{−1/2}. For a flat matter-plus-Λ model this integrates to (2/3)(1 − Ωm)^{−1/2} sinh⁻¹[((1 − Ωm)/Ωm)^{1/2}], about 0.96 Hubble times for Ωm = 0.3, compared with 2/3 for the Einstein-de Sitter model.
concepts.how_introduced: Separating variables in the dimensionless Friedmann equation and integrating from R̃ = 0 to 1; §26.5 uses the result to argue that Λ relieves the tension with ages of old stars.

concepts.name: Hubble constant
concepts.definition: Present value of the expansion rate Ṙ/R, an inverse time conventionally quoted in km/s per Mpc. The book quotes 72 ± 8 and writes H0 = 100h km/s/Mpc with h = 0.72 ± 0.08.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens §26.2 as the first of the four parameters to be measured; the text explains why measurement is difficult rather than presenting data.
concepts.notes: Dated: modern values cluster near 67-68 from the CMB and near 73 from the distance ladder (the 'Hubble tension').

concepts.name: parsec and megaparsec
concepts.definition: The parsec is the distance at which one astronomical unit (the Earth-Sun distance) subtends one arcsecond, 3.08×10¹⁶ m ≈ 3.26 light years; a megaparsec is 10⁶ pc, of the order of inter-galaxy distances in the Local Group.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced with a table of order-of-magnitude distance scales to give a feel for H0's units.
concepts.notes: The book's wording uses the width of Earth's orbit, which would correspond to the diameter rather than the radius.

concepts.name: peculiar velocity
aliases: motion relative to the Hubble flow
concepts.definition: A galaxy's velocity relative to the smooth cosmic expansion, produced by local gravitational attractions. For nearby galaxies it can rival the expansion velocity, spoiling redshift-based distance estimates.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the reason H0 must be measured with distant objects.

concepts.name: standard candle
concepts.definition: A class of source assumed to have the same intrinsic luminosity everywhere and at every epoch, so its apparent brightness yields its luminosity distance. The book names main-sequence stars, Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the way to obtain distances of objects too far for parallax.

concepts.name: cosmic distance ladder
concepts.definition: A chain of overlapping distance methods in which directly measured nearby distances calibrate the true brightness of standard candles that reach farther, which in turn calibrate still brighter candles.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the calibration problem: one needs not only that candles are identical but their actual luminosity, and there may be no example close enough to measure directly.

concepts.name: Hubble's law
concepts.definition: For nearby galaxies redshift is proportional to distance, z ≈ H0 d_L; it holds only to first order and must be replaced by the exact d_L(z) relation for distant sources.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 24 as the naive route to H0 and as the approximation superseded in §26.4.

concepts.name: luminosity distance
concepts.definition: In the book's convention, the distance inferred from received flux of a source of known power with redshift losses divided out; in a Robertson-Walker universe it equals r1R(t0), the present areal radius of the sphere through the observer centred on the source.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from (24.72) at the start of the supernova argument.
concepts.notes: Most modern texts define d_L = (1+z)R0 r1; the book's d_L is what they call the transverse comoving distance.

concepts.name: comoving radial coordinate χ
concepts.definition: χ = ∫_{t1}^{t0} dt/R(t), the coordinate distance covered by a radial light ray between emission and reception; the source's radial coordinate is r1 = sin χ, χ or sinh χ for k = +1, 0, −1.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in the exact luminosity-distance derivation and, as ∫dr = ∫dt/R, in the particle-horizon calculation.
prerequisites: null geodesics in the Robertson-Walker metric

concepts.name: exact luminosity distance-redshift relation
concepts.definition: For matter plus Λ, d_L(z) = R0 sin(g/R0), g, or R0 sinh(g/R0) for k = +1, 0, −1, where g(z) = H0⁻¹∫_{(1+z)⁻¹}^1 dR̃/(R̃[Ωc − 2V(R̃)]^{1/2}) and R0 = 1/(H0|Ωc|^{1/2}). Fitting it to distant supernovae constrains a combination of Ωm and ΩΛ.
concepts.how_introduced: Needed because the linear Hubble law of Chapter 24 rests on approximations that fail for distant supernovae; derived by changing variable from t to R̃ in χ and inserting the dimensionless Friedmann equation.
prerequisites: effective potential for the scale factor

concepts.name: cosmic microwave background
concepts.definition: Nearly perfectly isotropic black-body radiation at T0 = 2.725 K filling the universe: thermal radiation released when the universe became transparent and redshifted by about a factor 1000 since. It is evidence for a hot big bang and for large-scale isotropy, and it fixes Ωr.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the gateway to Ωr and as observational justification of the Robertson-Walker metric, with the story of its prediction and detection.

concepts.name: black-body spectrum
concepts.definition: Energy density per unit frequency of radiation in thermal equilibrium, f(ν) = (8πh/c³) ν³/(e^{hν/k_BT} − 1). In x = hν/k_BT it peaks at x ≈ 2.82; the mean photon energy is about 2.7 k_BT.
concepts.how_introduced: Imported from statistical physics (Level 2) with a dimensionless plot; its peak and mean are used for the decoupling estimate.
concepts.notes: The book quotes E_max ≈ 2.7k_BT and E_mean ≈ 3k_BT, and its printed stationarity condition lacks a factor e^x.

concepts.name: radiation energy density law
concepts.definition: Integrating the Planck spectrum over frequency gives total radiation energy density ε = αT⁴ with α = π²k_B⁴/(15ħ³c³) = 7.565×10⁻¹⁶ J m⁻³ K⁻⁴.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by the substitution y = hν/k_BT (Exercise 26.8) and applied at T0 to give ε ≈ 4.17×10⁻¹⁴ J m⁻³ and ΩCMB ≈ 5×10⁻⁵.

concepts.name: temperature-redshift relation
concepts.definition: Because radiation energy density falls as R⁻⁴ and equals αT⁴, the radiation temperature scales as 1/R: the universe was 1000 times hotter when 1000 times smaller, and T/T0 = 1 + z.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by combining (26.36) with the R⁻⁴ law; singled out by the authors as one of the two results to retain from the Level 2 material.
prerequisites: scaling of densities with the scale factor

concepts.name: preservation of the black-body form under expansion
concepts.definition: A thermal spectrum stays thermal as the universe expands: every frequency and the temperature both scale as 1/R, so hν/k_BT is unchanged, while the ν³ prefactor rescales exactly like inverse volume. A black body at decoupling is therefore a black body today at a lower temperature.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as a worry (the temperature changes, so why should old radiation still look thermal?) and resolved by the scaling argument; used to explain why the CMB is such a perfect black body.

concepts.name: decoupling
concepts.definition: The rather quick change, at T ≈ 3000 K when the universe was about a thousandth of its present size, from an opaque ionized plasma in which photons scatter constantly to a transparent gas of neutral atoms through which CMB photons travel freely.
concepts.how_introduced: Modelled with hydrogen plus photons; a crude estimate from 3k_BT = 14 eV (about 50,000 K) is corrected by the high-energy tail of the spectrum and the large number of photons per atom.
concepts.notes: Standard texts distinguish recombination (atoms form) from photon decoupling; the book merges them and rounds hydrogen's 13.6 eV ionization energy to 14 eV.

concepts.name: photon-to-baryon ratio
concepts.definition: Number of photons per baryon, very large in our universe (about 10⁹, a figure not given in the book). Because of it, the rare photons in the spectral tail can keep hydrogen ionized until k_BT is far below the ionization energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the second reason the crude decoupling estimate is too high by about ten.

concepts.name: last scattering surface
concepts.definition: The sphere, centred on a given observer, on which the CMB photons now arriving were last scattered at decoupling. It is not a physical shell: every point emitted at decoupling, and observers at other places or epochs see other spheres. For us its radius is thousands of Mpc.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced right after decoupling with an emphasis on its observer dependence; used in §26.7 to state the horizon problem.

concepts.name: CMB anisotropies and angular power spectrum
concepts.definition: Tiny direction-dependent temperature variations of the CMB, summarized by the correlation C(θ) between temperatures a fixed angle apart and decomposed into multipoles ℓ (angular scale roughly 180°/ℓ). Peak positions and heights depend on spatial geometry and on baryon, dark matter and dark energy content.
concepts.how_introduced: Described qualitatively as the second decisive constraint on the model plane, with the Planck 2013 spectrum; in §26.7 their origin is attributed to inflated quantum fluctuations.

concepts.name: big bang nucleosynthesis
concepts.definition: Formation of the light nuclei (deuterium, helium, lithium) in the hot early universe, well before decoupling because nuclear binding energies far exceed atomic ones. Predicted abundances depend on the baryon number density, and matching observations requires Ω_baryon ≈ 0.04.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as an independent route to the ordinary-matter density after star counts fall short.

concepts.name: baryon density parameter
concepts.definition: Fraction of the critical density in ordinary matter made of protons and neutrons, about 0.04 from nucleosynthesis: four times the 0.01 in stars but about a seventh of Ωm ≈ 0.3.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to show that most ordinary matter is dark and that most matter is non-baryonic.

concepts.name: galaxy rotation curve
concepts.definition: Orbital speed of stars and gas plotted against radius r in a galaxy. Newtonian circular orbits give v = √(GM(r)/r), so outside the visible mass v should fall like r^{−1/2}; observed curves stay roughly flat, implying M(r) ∝ r in an unseen halo.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from F = ma for a circular orbit as the first clue to non-luminous matter.

concepts.name: dark matter
concepts.definition: Matter detected through gravity but emitting no light. Its favoured form, cold dark matter, is non-baryonic, moves slowly compared with light, and interacts with ordinary matter essentially only gravitationally; it supplies most of Ωm ≈ 0.3.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by rotation curves and by the gap between Ω_baryon and Ωm; candidates are surveyed in §26.5 and its role in structure formation is noted in §26.9.

concepts.name: dark matter candidates
concepts.definition: Proposed constituents of dark matter: primordial black holes (they must predate nucleosynthesis to escape the baryon bound), massive compact halo objects (seen in microlensing towards the Large Magellanic Cloud but too few), light massive neutrinos (relativistic, hence 'hot', and limited by mass bounds), axions (hypothetical light particles also motivated by QCD) and supersymmetric weakly interacting massive particles (sought by direct detection and accelerators). None is confirmed.
concepts.how_introduced: Surveyed in §26.5, first astrophysical then particle-physics options, ending with the admission that the answer may be something not yet imagined.

concepts.name: dark energy
concepts.definition: Whatever accounts for ΩΛ ≈ 0.7 and the present acceleration. It may be a geometric constant Λ needing no more explanation than G, the quantum vacuum's zero-point energy (a fluid with p = −ρ), a dynamical scalar field, or a sign of modified gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in the audit of ΛCDM with the two readings of the cosmological term (left or right side of Einstein's equations).
prerequisites: vacuum energy as a perfect fluid

concepts.name: cosmological constant problem
concepts.definition: If Λ is quantum zero-point energy, standard particle physics predicts a vacuum density more than a hundred orders of magnitude larger than observed.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the main difficulty of the vacuum-energy interpretation, with the hope that supersymmetry or string theory might fix it.
prerequisites: vacuum energy as a perfect fluid
concepts.notes: Often quoted as about 120 orders of magnitude.

concepts.name: quintessence
concepts.definition: An alternative to a strict cosmological constant in which dark energy is a slowly evolving scalar field φ in a potential V(φ).
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned among dark energy options, foreshadowing the scalar-field treatment of inflation.

concepts.name: averaging problem in cosmology
concepts.definition: Because Einstein's equations are non-linear, the spacetime obtained from a smoothed matter distribution need not equal the average of the true lumpy spacetime, so fitting a Robertson-Walker model to an inhomogeneous universe could bias inferred parameters such as ΩΛ.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised, citing Ellis (2011), as a theoretical objection to the inference of a cosmological constant.

concepts.name: ΛCDM model
concepts.definition: Spatially flat FRW model with a positive cosmological constant and cold dark matter, Ωm ≈ 0.3 and ΩΛ ≈ 0.7, radiation negligible except early, preceded by inflation. Once radiation is unimportant R̃ = (Ωm/ΩΛ)^{1/3} sinh^{2/3}(t/tΛ), passing from t^{2/3} deceleration to exponential de Sitter-like acceleration.
concepts.how_introduced: Identified in §26.4 where supernova and CMB constraints cross; §26.5 lists its successes, exact solution and unexplained ingredients; §26.9 recaps its full history.
prerequisites: CMB anisotropies and angular power spectrum

concepts.name: de Sitter expansion
concepts.definition: Expansion with constant Hubble rate, R ∝ e^{Ht}, produced when a cosmological constant (or anything with T_ab ∝ g_ab) dominates. It is the late-time fate of ΛCDM with H = H0√ΩΛ and the form of inflationary expansion.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 25 for the far future of ΛCDM and for slow-roll inflation.
prerequisites: vacuum energy as a perfect fluid

concepts.name: matter-radiation equality
concepts.definition: The epoch when radiation and matter densities are equal. Since ρr/ρm = (Ωr/Ωm)/R̃, it happens at R̃_eq = Ωr/Ωm ≈ 2×10⁻⁴, around 10¹² s (tens of thousands of years); radiation dominates before, matter after.
concepts.how_introduced: Found from the ratio of the two scaling laws with Ωr = 7×10⁻⁵, Ωm = 0.3.
prerequisites: scaling of densities with the scale factor

concepts.name: thermal history of the universe
concepts.definition: The sequence of states implied by T ∝ 1/R: free quarks and leptons before about 10⁻⁴ s, free nucleons until about 1 s (≈1 MeV), nuclei in a radiation-dominated plasma until about 10¹² s, a matter-dominated plasma until about 10¹³ s, and neutral atoms with free-streaming photons thereafter.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from two scaling laws and a few anchor values, then tabulated and illustrated.

concepts.name: temperature-time relation in the radiation era
concepts.definition: During radiation domination R ∝ t^{1/2} and T ∝ 1/R, so T ∝ t^{−1/2}; normalized at equality the book finds T ≈ 1.5×10¹⁰ K (t/1 s)^{−1/2}, i.e. about 1 MeV when the universe is one second old.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by changing the exponent in the matter-era relation and matching at t_eq; Exercise 26.9 derives it independently from ρr c² = αT⁴ and H = 1/2t.

concepts.name: quark-hadron phase transition
concepts.definition: Transition at energies of a few hundred MeV (T ~ 2×10¹² K, t ~ 10⁻⁴ s) above which protons and neutrons dissolve into free quarks.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the earliest epoch reached by the scaling argument.

concepts.name: flatness problem
concepts.definition: In decelerating expansion |1 − ρ/ρcrit(t)| = |k|/(HR)² grows with time (∝ t^{2/3} when matter dominates, ∝ t for radiation), so a universe near critical density today must have started absurdly close to it; the problem is to explain that tuning rather than assume it.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from a time-dependent critical density and extrapolated back from today's bound to matter-radiation equality and the quark-hadron epoch.

concepts.name: particle horizon
concepts.definition: The greatest proper distance from which a signal emitted at the big bang can have reached a given observer by time t, Δr = R(t)∫₀ᵗ dt'/R(t'). It equals 2t for R ∝ t^{1/2} but grows like e^{Ht}/H under exponential expansion.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Chapter 25 by integrating a radial null ray in a flat Robertson-Walker metric.

concepts.name: horizon problem
concepts.definition: CMB photons arriving from opposite directions left points on the last scattering surface whose past light cones, traced back to the big bang, do not overlap; nothing could have brought them to a common temperature, yet they agree to one part in 10⁴. In a standard hot big bang only patches within about 2° on the sky shared any causal past.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced through the everyday idea that homogeneity needs mixing, then the particle horizon integral and a light-cone picture.

concepts.name: cosmic inflation
concepts.definition: A hypothesized very early phase (as early as ~10⁻³⁴ s) of nearly exponential expansion that blows a small, causally connected, thermalized patch up beyond the present observable universe, dilutes irregularities, drives Ω towards 1, and turns quantum fluctuations into the seeds of structure.
concepts.how_introduced: Proposed as the common cure of the flatness and horizon problems by re-evaluating the very formulas that expose them for R ∝ e^{Ht}.

concepts.name: inflaton scalar field
concepts.definition: A scalar field with Lagrangian density √−g[−½g^{ab}∇aφ∇bφ + V(φ)] (book's sign convention, signature +−−−). It obeys □φ + V'(φ) = 0, reduces for a homogeneous field in an FRW background to φ̈ + 3Hφ̇ + V' = 0, and has energy-momentum tensor T_ab = ∇aφ∇bφ + g_ab[−½(∇φ)² + V].
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as one possible engine for inflation using the book's variational methods, with the field equation and T_ab left as Exercise 26.12.
prerequisites: variational derivation of the energy-momentum tensor

concepts.name: Hubble friction
concepts.definition: The 3Hφ̇ term in the homogeneous scalar-field equation, which acts like friction on a particle rolling in the potential V(φ); when H is large compared with the slope of V it keeps φ̇ small.
concepts.how_introduced: Pointed out by reading (26.66) as a damped particle equation.

concepts.name: slow-roll inflation
concepts.definition: Inflation driven by a scalar field on a nearly flat stretch of its potential, where Hubble friction keeps φ ≈ φ*. Its stress tensor is then T_ab ≈ V(φ*)g_ab, an effective cosmological constant giving de Sitter expansion, until φ reaches the steep part, falls to the minimum and the released energy reheats the universe into radiation domination.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the damped field equation and illustrated with a plateau-then-well potential.
prerequisites: vacuum energy as a perfect fluid
concepts.notes: The book gives H = (V/3)^{1/2}; with ρ = V and H² = 8πρ/3 one expects H = (8πV/3)^{1/2}. Reheating appears only as a figure label.

concepts.name: primordial density perturbations from inflation
concepts.definition: Quantum fluctuations δφ of the inflaton create density fluctuations δρ ≈ V'(φ*)δφ that inflation stretches to cosmic scales; they appear later as CMB anisotropies and seed galaxies, and the predicted spectrum shape agrees with data and constrains V.
concepts.how_introduced: Sketched briefly as a bonus of inflation beyond its original motivation.
prerequisites: CMB anisotropies and angular power spectrum

concepts.name: gravitational instability
concepts.definition: Growth of density contrasts: slightly overdense regions attract matter and grow denser, underdense regions empty out. Simulations reproduce observed galaxy clustering only when dark matter is included.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in the closing section as the mechanism the book has not treated.

concepts.name: anthropic principle
concepts.definition: The explanatory stance that observed features of the universe are constrained by the requirement that observers like us can exist in it.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as an alternative to inflation for why the cosmological principle holds.

concepts.name: weak anthropic principle
concepts.definition: In the book's version: only some regions or epochs of the universe allow life to develop, so we necessarily observe one of them. Example: we find the universe many billions of years old because galaxies, heavy elements, planets and evolution take that long.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in a highlighted panel and illustrated by the age argument.

concepts.name: strong anthropic principle
concepts.definition: In the book's version: of many separate universes (quantum branches, or disjoint regions with their own initial conditions or even laws) only a few allow life. Fine-tuned constants are then read as a selection effect rather than design.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated through quantum cosmology and many-worlds, then subjected to three objections.
concepts.notes: Differs from Barrow and Tipler's usage (the universe must have properties allowing life); the book follows Hawking (1988).

concepts.name: many-worlds interpretation
concepts.definition: Reading of quantum mechanics in which the universe continually splits into many non-interacting branches, one for each possible outcome.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned, with a branching-tree figure, as one route to many universes for the strong anthropic principle.

concepts.name: fine-tuning of fundamental constants
concepts.definition: The observation that unexplained constants appear finely adjusted: small changes would give universes unable to support life. It is interpreted either as evidence of design or as support for anthropic selection.
concepts.how_introduced: Raised as the evidence behind the strong anthropic principle.

concepts.name: Copernican principle
concepts.definition: The view that we occupy no privileged position: a typical planet, star, galaxy and cluster. The book frames this through the cosmological principle and uses it against the human-centred strong anthropic principle.
concepts.how_introduced: Cited as the historical trend that the strong anthropic principle would reverse.

concepts.name: arrows of time
concepts.definition: Distinct time directions: the thermodynamic arrow of increasing entropy, cosmological (world) time defined by expansion, and psychological time as experienced; anthropic reasoning is suggested as a way to ask why they agree.
concepts.how_introduced: Brief mention at the end of the anthropic discussion, following Hawking (1988).

concepts.name: quantum cosmology
concepts.definition: Application of quantum theory to the universe as a whole, required for the earliest epochs and entangled with the interpretation problems of quantum mechanics.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as the setting in which many-worlds ideas arise.

concepts.name: big bang singularity
concepts.definition: The initial state as R → 0 where density and temperature grow without bound and spacetime itself ceases to be defined. The singularity theorems suggest it is generic rather than an artefact of exact symmetry, and unlike black-hole singularities it is in principle observable.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited in the closing recap, with the question whether inhomogeneities could replace it by a bounce.

concepts.name: singularity theorems
concepts.definition: Results showing, under energy conditions, that singularities (incomplete geodesics) are generic in gravitational collapse and cosmology, not consequences of symmetry assumptions.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked against the idea that local irregularities would prevent the initial singularity.

concepts.name: multi-messenger astronomy
concepts.definition: Study of astrophysical sources and the universe by combining gravitational-wave signals with electromagnetic observations in radio, optical and X-ray bands.
concepts.how_introduced: Heralded in the closing section together with the planned space detector LISA.

concepts.name: steady-state theory
concepts.definition: A model of an eternally unchanging expanding universe with continuous creation of matter. The book notes it predicted a background spectrum with much more high-frequency energy than the observed black body.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited briefly as the loser in the comparison of CMB spectra.

concepts.name: conformal cyclic cosmology
concepts.definition: Penrose's proposal of an endless sequence of aeons in which the conformally rescaled remote future of one universe becomes the big bang of the next; cited in the book only as an alternative to inflation.
concepts.how_introduced: One-line mention among possible new ideas.
concepts.notes: Description beyond the book's single mention.

key_equations.name: Friedmann equation with Λ = 0
key_equations.meaning: Squared Hubble rate balances density against spatial curvature; the starting point for defining the critical density.
key_equations.symbols: H = Ṙ/R; ρ density; k curvature index; R scale factor (G = c = 1)

key_equations.name: Critical density
key_equations.meaning: Present density that would make k = 0; of order 10⁻²⁶ kg m⁻³.

key_equations.name: Density and spatial geometry
key_equations.latex: \rho_0>\rho_{\rm crit}\Rightarrow k=+1,\quad \rho_0=\rho_{\rm crit}\Rightarrow k=0,\quad \rho_0<\rho_{\rm crit}\Rightarrow k=-1
key_equations.meaning: For Λ = 0 the actual density compared with critical decides closed, flat or open.

key_equations.name: Density parameter
key_equations.meaning: Present density in units of the critical density; Ω > 1 closed, = 1 flat, < 1 open (Λ = 0).

key_equations.name: Vacuum energy density
key_equations.meaning: The cosmological constant behaves as a fluid of constant density with negative pressure.

key_equations.name: Multi-component Friedmann equation
key_equations.meaning: Expansion rate set by radiation, matter and vacuum densities plus curvature.
key_equations.symbols: ρr, ρm, ρΛ radiation, matter, vacuum densities

key_equations.name: Dimensionless scale factor and time
key_equations.meaning: Measure size relative to today and time in Hubble times.

key_equations.name: Component density parameters
key_equations.meaning: Present fractions of critical density in radiation, matter and vacuum energy.

key_equations.name: Densities in terms of Ω and R̃
key_equations.meaning: Matter dilutes with volume, radiation also redshifts, vacuum energy is constant. (The reading copy's OCR shows a dotted R in (26.10)-(26.11); the printed page has R̃.)

key_equations.name: Dimensionless Friedmann equation
key_equations.meaning: All dynamics in terms of present-day parameters; H0 appears only in the curvature term through R0.

key_equations.name: Curvature parameter
key_equations.meaning: Curvature term expressed as an effective density fraction; positive for open models.

key_equations.name: Sum rule
key_equations.meaning: Evaluating (26.13) at R̃ = 1: curvature is determined by measurable contents.

key_equations.name: Particle-in-a-potential form
key_equations.latex: \tfrac12\left(\frac{d\tilde R}{d\tilde t}\right)^2+V(\tilde R)=E,\quad V(\tilde R)=-\tfrac12\left(\frac{\Omega_m}{\tilde R}+\frac{\Omega_r}{\tilde R^2}+\Omega_\Lambda\tilde R^2\right),\quad 2E=\Omega_c
key_equations.meaning: Expansion as one-dimensional motion of a unit mass; turning points where V = E.
key_equations.symbols: V effective potential; E effective energy

key_equations.name: Quadrature for R̃(t̃)
key_equations.meaning: Separable integral giving time as a function of scale factor.

key_equations.name: Restoring dimensions (corrected argument)
key_equations.meaning: H0 and R0 merely rescale the dimensionless solution. The printed equations and Exercise 26.6 write the argument as t̃/H0; since t̃ = H0t it should be H0t (or t̃).

key_equations.name: Potential and energy with Ωr = 0
key_equations.meaning: Two-parameter version used to map the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane.

key_equations.name: Present deceleration parameter
key_equations.meaning: Acceleration today iff ΩΛ > Ωm/2.

key_equations.name: Slope of the potential
key_equations.meaning: Vanishes at R̃³ = Ωm/2ΩΛ, the top of the barrier.

key_equations.name: Height of the barrier
key_equations.meaning: Maximum of V for positive Ωm and ΩΛ.

key_equations.name: Boundary condition E = V_max
key_equations.meaning: Curve in the model plane separating bounce/recollapse behaviour from monotonic expansion.

key_equations.name: Cubic for the boundary
key_equations.meaning: Obtained by cubing (26.27) with x = Ωm, y = ΩΛ; its roots through (0,1) and (1,0) are the physical boundaries. Cubing can introduce spurious branches, so solutions must be checked against (26.27).

key_equations.name: Age of the universe
key_equations.meaning: Time since R = 0 in Hubble times.

key_equations.name: Age of a flat matter-plus-Λ universe
key_equations.meaning: Closed form of (26.29) with ΩΛ = 1 − Ωm; 0.964 for Ωm = 0.3 (my evaluation), tending to 2/3 as Ωm → 1.

key_equations.name: Hubble constant (book's value)
key_equations.meaning: Recession speed per unit distance; dated estimate.

key_equations.name: h-parameterization
key_equations.meaning: Carries the uncertainty of H0 as a dimensionless factor.

key_equations.name: CMB temperature
key_equations.meaning: Present black-body temperature of the background radiation.

key_equations.name: Planck spectrum
key_equations.meaning: Energy density of thermal radiation per unit frequency and in total.
key_equations.symbols: h Planck's constant; k_B Boltzmann's constant; ν frequency

key_equations.name: Peak of the Planck spectrum (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Setting f'(ν) = 0. The printed condition reads like 3(e^x − 1) = x (with a misplaced parenthesis), which has no positive root; the correct form is 3(e^x − 1) = xe^x. The book quotes ν_max ≈ 2.7k_BT/h and E_mean ≈ 3k_BT; the precise values are 2.82 and 2.70.

key_equations.name: Radiation energy density
key_equations.meaning: Total thermal radiation energy grows as the fourth power of temperature.

key_equations.name: Radiation density parameter
key_equations.meaning: CMB photons plus neutrinos (and possibly gravitons) contribute a negligible fraction today.

key_equations.name: Temperature scaling
key_equations.meaning: The universe cools inversely with its size.

key_equations.name: Crude decoupling estimate
key_equations.meaning: Mean photon energy equal to hydrogen's ionization energy; about ten times too high.

key_equations.name: Decoupling temperature
key_equations.meaning: Realistic value accounting for the spectral tail and the photon excess.

key_equations.name: Rotation curve
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian circular orbit speed; flat observed v(r) implies M(r) ∝ r.
key_equations.symbols: M(r) mass within r; ω angular velocity

key_equations.name: Estimated matter fractions
key_equations.meaning: Luminous matter versus all ordinary matter from nucleosynthesis.

key_equations.name: Source coordinate from a light ray
key_equations.meaning: Radial coordinate of an emitter from the conformal-time interval along the ray.

key_equations.name: Changing variables in χ (corrected first line)
key_equations.latex: \chi=\int_{R(t_1)}^{R(t_0)}\frac{dR}{\dot R\,R}=\frac{1}{R_0H_0}\int_{(1+z)^{-1}}^{1}\frac{d\tilde R}{\tilde R\,(d\tilde R/d\tilde t)}=\frac{1}{R_0H_0}\int_{(1+z)^{-1}}^{1}\frac{d\tilde R}{\tilde R\left[\Omega_c-2V(\tilde R)\right]^{1/2}}
key_equations.meaning: Time integral turned into an integral over the scale factor using the Friedmann equation; the printed first integrand shows R̃(r)R where ṘR is meant.

key_equations.name: Exact luminosity distance
key_equations.latex: g(z):=\frac{1}{H_0}\int_{(1+z)^{-1}}^{1}\frac{d\tilde R}{\tilde R[\Omega_c-2V(\tilde R)]^{1/2}},\qquad d_L(z)=\begin{cases}R_0\sin(g/R_0)&k=+1\\ g(z)&k=0\\ R_0\sinh(g/R_0)&k=-1\end{cases},\quad R_0=\frac{1}{H_0|\Omega_c|^{1/2}}
key_equations.meaning: d_L versus z for any (Ωm, ΩΛ); comparison with Type Ia supernovae constrains the model plane. Uses the book's d_L without the usual (1+z) factor.

key_equations.name: ΛCDM scale factor
key_equations.meaning: Exact flat matter-plus-Λ solution (normalized so R = 1 today): t^{2/3} early, e^{H0√ΩΛ t} late.
key_equations.symbols: R here is the normalized R̃

key_equations.name: Radiation-to-matter ratio
key_equations.meaning: Radiation gains on matter by one power of 1/R̃ going back in time.

key_equations.name: Matter-radiation equality
key_equations.meaning: With Ωr = 7×10⁻⁵, Ωm = 0.3.

key_equations.name: Temperature-time law, matter era
key_equations.meaning: Combines T ∝ 1/R with R ∝ t^{2/3}; order-of-magnitude only since it ignores the Λ era.

key_equations.name: Decoupling and equality times
key_equations.latex: t_{\rm dec}\sim10^{13}\,{\rm s}\ (\sim3.5\times10^5\,{\rm yr}),\qquad t_{\rm eq}\simeq10^{12}\,{\rm s}\ (\simeq3.5\times10^4\,{\rm yr})
key_equations.meaning: From (26.51) with T/T0 ≈ 1000 and ≈ 5000, t0 = 4×10¹⁷ s. The printed (26.52) has a missing coefficient before ×10¹³; the scaling gives 1.3×10¹³ s ≈ 4×10⁵ yr (my evaluation).

key_equations.name: Temperature-time law, radiation era
key_equations.latex: \frac{T(t)}{T_{\rm eq}}=\left(\frac{t_{\rm eq}}{t}\right)^{1/2},\qquad T(t)\simeq\frac{1.5\times10^{10}}{\sqrt t}\ \ (T\ {\rm in\ K},\ t\ {\rm in\ s})
key_equations.meaning: About 10¹⁰ K (1 MeV) at one second. The book's T_eq ≈ 30,000 K is not consistent with R̃_eq ≈ 2×10⁻⁴ (which gives ≈14,000 K); the coefficient nevertheless agrees with a direct radiation-era calculation.

key_equations.name: Deviation from critical density
key_equations.meaning: Since HR = Ṙ, the departure from critical density is |k|/Ṙ²: it grows whenever the expansion decelerates and shrinks when it accelerates.

key_equations.name: Growth of the flatness deviation
key_equations.meaning: Deviation grows during matter domination, so it must have been tiny early.

key_equations.name: Radial null ray
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate distance travelled by light in a flat RW universe.

key_equations.name: Proper horizon distance
key_equations.meaning: With t1 = 0, t2 = t: radius of the particle horizon.

key_equations.name: Horizon in a radiation era
key_equations.meaning: Horizon grows only linearly (twice the naive ct).

key_equations.name: Horizon during inflation
key_equations.latex: R=Ae^{\tilde Ht}\ \Rightarrow\ \Delta r(t)=e^{\tilde Ht}\int_0^te^{-\tilde Hu}du=\frac{e^{\tilde Ht}-1}{\tilde H}
key_equations.meaning: Horizon grows exponentially. The printed intermediate bracket shows e^{H̃u} instead of e^{−H̃u}.

key_equations.name: Flatness during inflation
key_equations.meaning: Exponential expansion drives the universe towards critical density.

key_equations.name: Scalar-field action and Lagrangian density
key_equations.meaning: Action for the inflaton in the book's sign conventions.
key_equations.symbols: Ω integration region (not a density parameter)

key_equations.name: Scalar field equation
key_equations.meaning: Euler-Lagrange equation from δℒ/δφ = 0 (Exercise 26.12(i)).

key_equations.name: Homogeneous inflaton in FRW
key_equations.meaning: Damped particle-like equation; 3Hφ̇ is Hubble friction.

key_equations.name: Energy-momentum from the action
key_equations.meaning: Metric variation defines the source tensor.

key_equations.name: Scalar-field energy-momentum tensor
key_equations.meaning: Gives ρ = ½φ̇² + V and p = ½φ̇² − V.

key_equations.name: Slow-roll limit
key_equations.meaning: A frozen field acts like a cosmological constant.

key_equations.name: Inflationary expansion rate
key_equations.meaning: de Sitter expansion from the potential energy. With ρ = V and H² = 8πρ/3 (consistent with (26.5)) one expects H̃ = (8πV/3)^{1/2}; the printed form treats V as Λ.

key_equations.name: Density fluctuation from inflaton fluctuation
key_equations.meaning: Quantum jitter in φ becomes density perturbations that inflation stretches.

figures.label: Fig. 26.1 (left panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Effective potential for the scale factor when the barrier lies below the energy level.
figures.visual_description: Axes: R̃ horizontal from 0 to 3, V(R̃) vertical from −3 to 1. A thin horizontal line at V = 0 is labelled E. The black curve rises from far below near R̃ = 0 to a rounded maximum of about −0.4 near R̃ ≈ 0.6, then falls steadily, passing −3 near R̃ ≈ 2.9. The curve stays entirely below the E line. (The shape matches Ωm = 0.3, ΩΛ = 0.7, where V_max ≈ −0.38 at R̃ ≈ 0.60 and V(3) ≈ −3.2; my reconstruction.)
figures.what_it_teaches: When E exceeds V everywhere there is no turning point, so the model expands monotonically from a big bang; the flat concordance model is of this kind.
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor

redesign.idea: Linked potential and history explorer: V(R̃) with its E line beside the live-integrated R̃(t̃) curve, with a bead sliding along the potential in sync with a cursor on the history.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for Ωm, ΩΛ (and optionally Ωr); E updates from the sum rule; forbidden regions V > E are shaded; pressing play animates the bead and draws R̃(t̃), q, and the present epoch marker at R̃ = 1.

figures.label: Fig. 26.1 (right panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Effective potential when the barrier rises above the energy level, creating two turning points.
figures.visual_description: Same vertical scale as the left panel but R̃ runs from 0 to 10 with no vertical tick labels. A horizontal E line sits near V ≈ −0.5. The curve climbs steeply from R̃ ≈ 0, crosses the E line near R̃ ≈ 2, peaks slightly above it (about −0.45) around R̃ ≈ 3.5-4, recrosses near R̃ ≈ 6, and declines slowly to about −1.1 at R̃ = 10. (Consistent with Ωm ≈ 2, ΩΛ ≈ 0.02, my reconstruction.)
figures.what_it_teaches: A barrier above E splits motion into a region near R̃ = 0 (big bang then big crunch) and a region at large R̃ (contraction to a minimum and re-expansion, no big bang).
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor

redesign.idea: Two-basin demo: the learner drops the bead either left or right of the barrier and sees the resulting crunch or bounce history, then drags ΩΛ to lower the barrier until the two basins merge.
redesign.interaction: Click to set initial R̃ and direction of motion; ΩΛ slider moves the barrier; the R̃(t̃) inset redraws; the corresponding point moves across the no-big-bang boundary on a mini (Ωm, ΩΛ) map.

figures.label: Fig. 26.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Map of Friedmann-Robertson-Walker models in the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane (reproduced from Liddle).
figures.visual_description: Square plot with Ωm from 0 to 3 horizontally and ΩΛ from −1 to 3 vertically. Four labelled curves: a straight line from (0, 1) down to (2, −1) marked Closed above and Open below; a straight line from the origin to (3, 1.5) marked Accelerating above and Decelerating below; a nearly horizontal curve hugging ΩΛ = 0 from the origin and rising gently to about 0.2 at Ωm = 3, marked Expands forever above and Recollapses below; and a steep concave curve from (0, 1) reaching ΩΛ = 3 near Ωm ≈ 1.3, marked No Big Bang on its upper-left side.
figures.what_it_teaches: Qualitative properties of a universe (geometry, acceleration, fate, origin) are decided by where two measurable numbers place it relative to three boundaries, and these properties are independent of one another once Λ ≠ 0.

redesign.idea: Universe atlas: a clickable model plane whose boundary curves are computed live (including numerically solved V_max = E curves), with a side panel showing the chosen universe's R̃(t̃), q0, age and fate.
redesign.interaction: Click or drag a point; the panel updates; toggles highlight each boundary and explain which inequality it encodes; a 'tour' mode moves the point across each line to show the qualitative change.

figures.label: Table 26.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Rough orders of magnitude of distances in cosmology, in parsecs and light years.
figures.visual_description: Three-column table (not exported as an image; read from the rendered page). Rows: distance to the Sun 5×10⁻⁶ pc; nearest star 1 pc; galactic centre 10⁴ pc; local group 5×10⁵ pc; nearest large cluster 2×10⁷ pc; scale of largest structures 10⁸ pc; edge of the visible universe 1.4×10¹⁰ pc; each also in light years (1.5×10⁻⁵ to 5×10¹⁰).
figures.what_it_teaches: Cosmology spans more than fifteen decades of distance; megaparsecs are the natural unit for galaxy recession.

redesign.idea: Powers-of-ten zoom: a logarithmic scroll from the Earth-Sun distance to the observable universe with the table's landmarks as stops, echoing the Eames film the authors recommend.
redesign.interaction: Scroll or drag a log slider; landmarks fade in with distance, light-travel time and recession velocity at H0 = 70.

figures.label: Fig. 26.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Shape of the black-body energy distribution.
figures.visual_description: Single smooth curve. Horizontal axis hν/k_BT from 0 to 10; vertical axis the scaled spectrum f(ν)·c³h²/(8πk_B³T³) from 0 to 1.5 (axis label typeset with a capital K). The curve starts at zero, rises roughly like x², peaks at about 1.42 near x ≈ 2.8, and decays in a long tail to about 0.05 at x = 10.
figures.what_it_teaches: In dimensionless units every black body has the same shape; most energy sits near a few k_BT, but a long high-energy tail exists, which matters for decoupling.

redesign.idea: Black-body lab: plot the spectrum against physical frequency with a temperature slider, marking peak, mean energy and the 13.6 eV ionization threshold, plus a 'cosmic expansion' slider that redshifts every frequency and shows the curve remains a black body at T/a.
redesign.interaction: Drag T from 2.7 K to 10⁵ K; drag expansion factor; readouts give εrad = αT⁴, ΩCMB for the chosen T0, and the number of ionizing photons per hydrogen atom for a chosen photon-to-baryon ratio.

figures.label: Fig. 26.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: CMB temperature power spectrum from Planck 2013 (Ade et al. 2014).
figures.visual_description: Data points with error bars and a solid best-fit curve. Horizontal axis 'Multipole moment (ℓ)' from 2 to 2500, logarithmic up to 50 and linear beyond; a top axis gives angular scale 90°, 18°, 1°, 0.2°, 0.1°, 0.07°. Vertical axis D_ℓ in μK² from 0 to 6000. At low ℓ points scatter around 1000 with large error bars inside a grey band. The curve rises to a dominant peak of about 5700 near ℓ ≈ 220 (about 1°), then smaller peaks near ℓ ≈ 540 and 810 (each about 2400-2500), and progressively damped bumps near 1100 and 1400, falling towards zero by 2500.
figures.what_it_teaches: The pattern of temperature fluctuations on the sky has a characteristic angular scale and a series of peaks whose positions and heights encode the geometry and content of the universe.
concepts: CMB anisotropies and angular power spectrum

redesign.idea: Toy acoustic-peak explorer: a simplified model where total density shifts the first peak's ℓ, baryon fraction changes the odd/even peak heights, and matter density changes the damping, shown next to a simulated sky patch whose hot and cold spot sizes change accordingly.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for Ω_total, Ω_baryon, Ω_cdm; hover links ℓ to angle; a toggle overlays the real Planck points; clearly labelled as illustrative rather than a Boltzmann-code computation.

figures.label: Fig. 26.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Supernova and CMB constraints on the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane (reproduced from Liddle).
figures.visual_description: Same axes as Fig. 26.2 (Ωm 0 to about 2.8, ΩΛ −1 to 3). Upper-left dark grey region labelled No Big Bang; a pale grey region below a dashed line labelled Accelerating/Decelerating; a thin curve near ΩΛ = 0 labelled Expands to infinity above and Recollapses (dotted) below. Nested elongated contours at 68.3%, 95.4% and 99.7% run diagonally from lower left to upper right: solid for the High-Z SN Search Team, dashed for the Supernova Cosmology Project. A dark diagonal band labelled Boomerang+MAXIMA runs along the Closed/Open line from near (0, 1) down to about (1.9, −1). The SN contours and the CMB band intersect near Ωm ≈ 0.3, ΩΛ ≈ 0.7.
figures.what_it_teaches: Each probe alone allows a long degenerate strip, but because the strips are nearly perpendicular their intersection fixes a flat, accelerating universe with Ωm ≈ 0.3.
concepts: CMB anisotropies and angular power spectrum

redesign.idea: Two strips, one point: compute a supernova likelihood from synthetic d_L(z) data using (26.45)-(26.46) and overlay a CMB flatness band, letting the learner see why each constrains a different combination.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for SN redshift range, number of supernovae and magnitude error; a slider for CMB precision; contours redraw; a 'true universe' marker can be moved to generate new synthetic data.

figures.label: Table 26.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Stages in the evolution of the universe for Ωm = 0.3, H0 = 72.
figures.visual_description: Two-column table (not exported as an image; read from the rendered page): time interval versus state of matter. 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻⁴ s: free quarks, neutrinos, photons, electrons, all strongly interacting. 10⁻⁴ to 1 s: free electrons, protons, neutrons, photons, neutrinos. 1 to 10¹² s: electrons, nuclei, photons, neutrinos, radiation dominated. 10¹² to 10¹³ s: same, matter dominated. 10¹³ s to t0: atoms formed, photons free, transparent. t0 = 4×10¹⁷ s.
figures.what_it_teaches: Cosmic history can be organized by temperature thresholds matched to particle binding energies, with two dynamical transitions (equality, decoupling).

redesign.idea: Cosmic clock and thermometer: a log-time slider driving a readout of temperature, k_BT in eV, scale factor, dominant component and particle inventory, with the table's rows lighting up.
redesign.interaction: Drag time from 10⁻¹⁰ s to 4×10¹⁷ s; toggle between the book's piecewise power laws and a numerical integration including Λ to see how rough the estimates are.

figures.label: Fig. 26.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Illustrated history of the universe from the big bang to the present.
figures.visual_description: A vertical goblet- or trumpet-shaped artwork widening upward from a thin stem at the bottom. Left-hand time labels from bottom to top: 10⁻⁴³ s, 10⁻³⁸ s, 10⁻¹⁰ s, 0.001 s, 3 minutes, 500,000 years, 1 billion years, present. Era labels inside: Planck, GUT, electroweak, particle, nucleosynthesis, nuclei, atoms, galaxies. The lower part is filled with dense dots and small rings suggesting particles and nuclei, a darker band marks the atomic era, and the top is dark with stars and galaxies; faint ellipses mark horizontal slices at 1 billion years and the present.
figures.what_it_teaches: A qualitative, logarithmic-feeling timeline linking time since the big bang to what the universe contained; note it labels the atomic transition at 500,000 years, not the text's 350,000.

redesign.idea: Scrollable 3D cosmic history cone: the learner scrolls down through expanding cross-sections from today back to the Planck era, with particle populations, temperature and the observable-universe size changing, and the CMB release shown as fog clearing.
redesign.interaction: Scroll or drag time; click an era for a short explanation and the relevant equation; option to switch time axis between linear, logarithmic and scale factor.

figures.label: Fig. 26.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Light-cone sketch of the horizon problem.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing in perspective. A large cone opens downward from an apex dot labelled Earth (now), marked Past light cone, to a wide ellipse at the bottom labelled Initial singularity. Inside, several dots on or near the big cone are apexes of smaller downward cones whose own base ellipses are drawn on the singularity plane; some small cones nest inside medium ones. Dashed curves join pairs of dots and are labelled Causally disconnected events on both sides, pointing to apexes whose small cones' bases do not overlap.
figures.what_it_teaches: Points we see in different directions have past light cones that never intersect before the big bang, so no process could have equilibrated them.

redesign.idea: Conformal-diagram horizon lab: in conformal time versus comoving distance, draw our past light cone, the last scattering line and the past cones of two sky points; add an inflation phase that extends conformal time below zero.
redesign.interaction: Drag the angular separation of two sky points; the diagram highlights when their past cones overlap; a slider for inflation e-folds shows overlap appearing for all separations; readout of the causally connected angle (≈1-2° without inflation).

figures.label: Fig. 26.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Inflation enlarges a small thermalized patch beyond our observable universe.
figures.visual_description: A flared funnel or trumpet shape: a small pale ellipse at the bottom labelled Original small region, curved walls sweeping outward labelled INFLATION in the middle, and a large pale disc on top containing a darker central ellipse labelled Our universe.
