An upward arrow at the left is labelled Time.
figures.what_it_teaches: A region small enough to reach equilibrium before inflation can be stretched until our whole observable universe fits well inside it.

redesign.idea: Patch-and-horizon animation: a small mixed patch inside a Hubble sphere inflates while the Hubble radius stays fixed, then after inflation the observable universe's horizon grows but remains inside the inflated patch.
redesign.interaction: Scrub time; slider for number of e-folds shows the minimum (~60) needed to enclose today's horizon; colors show uniform temperature inside the patch.

figures.label: Fig. 26.9
figures.visual_description: Axes V(φ) vertical and φ horizontal. Starting at the vertical axis the curve is a flat plateau labelled Slow-roll inflation, then bends down smoothly into a minimum that touches V = 0, and rises steeply on the right; the minimum is labelled End of inflation → reheating.
figures.what_it_teaches: Inflation happens while the field creeps along a flat plateau (potential energy dominates); it ends when the field falls into the well and its energy is converted into radiation.

redesign.idea: Rolling-ball inflaton simulator: solve φ̈ + 3Hφ̇ + V' = 0 with H² = 8π(½φ̇² + V)/3, animating a ball on the potential alongside plots of ln R, H, and equation of state p/ρ.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for plateau height and flatness and initial φ; readouts of e-folds achieved and when p/ρ crosses −1/3; a toggle turns Hubble friction off to show why it matters.

figures.label: Fig. 26.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: Branching picture of the many-worlds interpretation.
figures.visual_description: A line drawing of a sideways tree: a short horizontal stem at the left splits into two diagonal branches, each of which splits repeatedly towards the right, ending in many short twigs. No labels or axes.
figures.what_it_teaches: Suggests a universe splitting into many disjoint histories at each quantum event.

redesign.idea: A simple branching animation is possible but adds little to the physics.

figures.label: Fig. 26.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: Wheeler's 'big U': the universe gives rise to observers who look back at its beginning.
figures.visual_description: A thick U-shaped tube drawn in outline. Its upper-right end flares into a narrow trumpet mouth (the big bang); the tube curves down and up the left side, ending in a circle containing a stylized eye that looks to the right along a horizontal dashed line back towards the trumpet end.
figures.what_it_teaches: Whimsical closing image of a universe that evolves observers capable of observing its origin, used to end the anthropic discussion and echo Lieber's book.

redesign.idea: Could be an end-of-course illustration but carries no quantitative content.

worked_examples.method: Insert H0 of order 100 km/s/Mpc into 3H0²/8π after restoring G (Exercise 26.2 repeats this with 1/H0 ≈ 10¹⁰ yr).
worked_examples.key_insight: The critical density is tiny in everyday terms yet comparable to the true cosmic mean, because intergalactic space is so empty.
worked_examples.result: ρcrit ~ 10⁻²⁶ kg m⁻³ (1.9×10⁻²⁶ for h = 1; 9.7×10⁻²⁷ for h = 0.72, my evaluation)

worked_examples.problem: Put the Friedmann equation with radiation, matter and Λ into dimensionless form and find the constraint on the present parameters.
worked_examples.method: Write each density as ρcrit Ω R̃⁻ⁿ, divide by H0², multiply by R̃², call the curvature term Ωc, then evaluate at R̃ = 1 where dR̃/dt̃ = 1 (Exercises 26.4-26.5).
worked_examples.key_insight: All present-day information collapses into Ω's that must add to one, so curvature is not an independent parameter.

worked_examples.problem: Reconstruct the physical scale factor R(t) from Ωr, Ωm, ΩΛ and H0.
worked_examples.method: Get E = Ωc/2; integrate t̃ = ∫dR̃/[2(E − V)]^{1/2} and invert; use |Ωc| = |k|/(H0R0)² with |k| = 1 to find R0 (Exercise 26.6).
worked_examples.key_insight: H0 only sets the units of time and, for curved models, the curvature radius; the Ω's decide the shape of the history.
worked_examples.result: R(t) = R0 R̃(H0t), R0 = 1/(H0|Ωc|^{1/2}); the printed argument t̃/H0 should read H0t
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor

worked_examples.problem: Express today's deceleration parameter through Ωm and ΩΛ.
worked_examples.method: Take q = (4πρ/3 − Λ/3)/H² from (24.79), substitute ρm(t0) = Ωmρcrit, Λ = 8πρΛ = 8πΩΛρcrit and ρcrit = 3H0²/8π.
worked_examples.key_insight: Matter brakes the expansion with half weight, vacuum energy accelerates it with full weight.
worked_examples.result: q0 = Ωm/2 − ΩΛ; acceleration boundary ΩΛ = Ωm/2; q0 = −0.55 for (0.3, 0.7)

worked_examples.problem: Find where in the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane the barrier of the effective potential just equals the energy.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate V = −½(Ωm/R̃ + ΩΛR̃²), solve for R̃³ = Ωm/2ΩΛ, substitute to get V_max = −¾(2Ωm²ΩΛ)^{1/3}, impose 2V_max = 1 − Ωm − ΩΛ, cube and collect a cubic in ΩΛ; keep the roots through (0, 1) and (1, 0) and discard the unphysical one.
worked_examples.key_insight: Turning-point analysis in a potential becomes a boundary between classes of universes in parameter space.
worked_examples.result: (26.27)-(26.28): no-big-bang curve from (0, 1); expand-forever/recollapse curve from (1, 0)
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor

worked_examples.problem: Compute the age of a flat universe containing matter and a cosmological constant.
worked_examples.method: Separate dR̃/dt̃ = [Ωm/R̃ + ΩΛR̃²]^{1/2}, integrate from 0 to 1; the substitution u = R̃^{3/2} reduces it to an inverse hyperbolic sine (Exercise 26.7). §26.5 then plugs in concordance values.
worked_examples.key_insight: Λ lengthens the age compared with the Einstein-de Sitter 2/3 Hubble time, easing conflict with old stars.
worked_examples.result: H0t0 = (2/3)(1 − Ωm)^{−1/2} sinh⁻¹√((1 − Ωm)/Ωm); for Ωm = 0.3 this is 0.964, about 13.1 Gyr at H0 = 72 (my evaluation; the book's 'Ωm = 0.7' would give 10.2 Gyr)

worked_examples.problem: Turn the measured CMB temperature into the present radiation density parameter.
worked_examples.method: Integrate the Planck spectrum with y = hν/k_BT to get αT⁴; evaluate at 2.725 K; divide by ρcrit c²; add neutrinos and possible gravitons.
worked_examples.key_insight: Radiation is negligible today, but because ρr/ρm ∝ 1/R̃ it dominated early.

worked_examples.problem: Estimate the temperature at which the universe became transparent.
worked_examples.method: Set the mean black-body photon energy 3k_BT equal to hydrogen's ionization energy (≈14 eV); then argue qualitatively that the high-energy tail and the vast number of photons per atom keep hydrogen ionized to much lower temperature.
worked_examples.key_insight: A threshold process in a photon-rich gas is controlled by the rare energetic photons, not the average one.
worked_examples.result: Crude 5×10⁴ K; realistic 3000 K, when R̃ ≈ 10⁻³; photons then at 1.6×10¹⁴ Hz, now 160 GHz

worked_examples.problem: Predict how orbital speed in a galaxy should depend on radius.
worked_examples.method: Equate the Newtonian attraction GmM(r)/r² to the centripetal force mrω² and use v = ωr.
worked_examples.key_insight: Outside the luminous mass v should fall as r^{−1/2}; flat observed curves require mass growing linearly with r in a dark halo.

worked_examples.problem: Derive the exact luminosity distance as a function of redshift for any (Ωm, ΩΛ).
worked_examples.method: Write r1 = sin χ, χ or sinh χ with χ = ∫dt/R; change variable to R and then R̃ = R/R0, t̃ = H0t; replace dR̃/dt̃ by [Ωc − 2V]^{1/2}; use 1 + z = R0/R(t1) for the lower limit; apply d_L = r1R0 and R0 = 1/(H0|Ωc|^{1/2}).
worked_examples.key_insight: The whole redshift-distance curve depends on the same effective potential that governs the dynamics, so supernova data map directly onto the model plane.
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor

worked_examples.problem: Rewrite the flat positive-Λ dust solution of Chapter 25 in terms of Ωm, ΩΛ and H0.
worked_examples.method: Express C and Λ through H0, Ωm, ΩΛ and verify the proposed sinh^{2/3} form satisfies Ṙ²/R² = H0²(Ωm/R³ + ΩΛ) (Exercise 26.10); expand for small and large t.
worked_examples.key_insight: One formula shows decelerating t^{2/3} growth giving way to exponential expansion at rate H0√ΩΛ.
worked_examples.result: R = (Ωm/ΩΛ)^{1/3} sinh^{2/3}(t/tΛ), tΛ = 2/(3H0√ΩΛ) ≈ 10.8 Gyr for H0 = 72, ΩΛ = 0.7 (my evaluation)

worked_examples.problem: Date matter-radiation equality and decoupling, and find the temperature-time law before equality.
worked_examples.method: Use ρr/ρm = (Ωr/Ωm)/R̃ to get R̃_eq; combine T ∝ 1/R̃ with R ∝ t^{2/3} so t = t0(T0/T)^{3/2}; for earlier times use R ∝ t^{1/2} and match at equality.
worked_examples.key_insight: Two scaling laws plus two anchor numbers give a usable cosmic calendar without solving the full equations.
worked_examples.result: R̃_eq ≈ 2×10⁻⁴; t_dec ~ 10¹³ s; t_eq ~ 10¹² s; T ≈ 1.5×10¹⁰ K/√t, about 1 MeV at 1 s
concepts: temperature-time relation in the radiation era

worked_examples.problem: Quantify how finely tuned the early density must have been.
worked_examples.method: Divide the Friedmann equation by H² to get |1 − Ω(t)| = |k|/(HR)²; with R ∝ t^{2/3}, H ∝ 1/t this grows as t^{2/3}; scale today's bound (0.3 at 4×10¹⁷ s) back to 10¹² s.
worked_examples.key_insight: Flatness is dynamically unstable in decelerating expansion, so near-flatness now is a clue, not a coincidence.
worked_examples.result: Book: below 10⁻⁵ at equality and far smaller earlier (a direct scaling of 0.3 gives about 5×10⁻⁵, my evaluation)

worked_examples.problem: Compare the particle horizon in radiation-dominated and exponentially expanding universes.
worked_examples.method: Evaluate Δr = R(t)∫₀ᵗdu/R(u) for R = At^{1/2} and for R = Ae^{H̃t}.
worked_examples.key_insight: Replacing a power law by an exponential changes horizon growth from linear to exponential, allowing distant regions to have been in contact.
worked_examples.result: Δr = 2t versus Δr = (e^{H̃t} − 1)/H̃; also |1 − Ω| ∝ e^{−2H̃t} during inflation

worked_examples.problem: Derive the dynamics and stress tensor of a homogeneous scalar field in an FRW universe and show when it mimics Λ.
worked_examples.method: Vary the Lagrangian density (26.65) with respect to φ and g^{ab}; specialize to φ = φ(t) in comoving coordinates where √−g ∝ R³; argue that large Hubble friction keeps φ̇ small (Exercise 26.12).
worked_examples.key_insight: A field frozen by Hubble friction has T_ab ∝ g_ab, exactly the form of a cosmological constant.
worked_examples.result: φ̈ + 3Hφ̇ + V' = 0; T_ab = δ⁰_aδ⁰_bφ̇² + g_ab(−½φ̇² + V); T_ab ≈ V(φ*)g_ab; R ∝ e^{H̃t}

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The scale factor behaves like a bead of unit mass moving along a line in a potential V(R̃), with total 'energy' fixed by the curvature parameter.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: effective potential for the scale factor
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Cosmic fates are read from where the E level meets the potential: no intersection means monotonic expansion from a big bang; intersections mean turning points, hence recollapse or a bounce. Also used to derive the no-big-bang boundary.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: E is not a physical energy of any system, R̃ = 0 is a singularity rather than a wall, time is dimensionless, and the picture applies only to exactly homogeneous models.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Bead on a potential curve synchronized with an R̃(t̃) plot; the learner changes Ω's and sees both update.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Ink dropped in water spreads until the glass is uniformly colored, because the parts have had time to mix.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Sets up the expectation that uniformity requires prior interaction, which particle horizons deny to widely separated regions of the early universe.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A glass of water has no horizons and is static; in the universe expansion can keep regions out of contact, and inflation produces uniformity by stretching a pre-mixed patch rather than by mixing across the observed sky.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-screen: diffusion in a box versus diffusion in an expanding box with a finite signal speed, showing mixing fail when expansion outruns it.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The inflaton is like a ball rolling down a hillside while immersed in a thick fluid whose drag is set by the Hubble rate.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why φ barely moves on a flat plateau (large friction), so its potential energy acts like a cosmological constant until the slope steepens.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The friction coefficient 3H itself depends on the field's energy, and quantum fluctuations and spatial gradients are ignored.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ball-on-potential simulator with a friction slider tied to H and a live e-fold counter.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Standard candles as light bulbs of known wattage: how dim one looks tells how far away it is.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains how luminosity distances are obtained for objects beyond parallax (the book uses the term without the bulb image).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Real candles may evolve with cosmic age or environment, dust dims them, and in cosmology the brightness-distance relation depends on the expansion history and the definition of d_L.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Drag identical bulbs to different distances and read flux; then switch on evolution or dust and see the inferred H0 bias.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A cosmic distance ladder: each rung is calibrated using the rung below it.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Describes the chain from parallax through Cepheids to supernovae that solves the calibration problem.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Errors propagate and accumulate up the ladder; different rungs overlap only partially.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Interactive ladder where the learner adjusts a calibration error on a low rung and watches the H0 estimate shift.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The multipole expansion of the CMB correlation function is like a Fourier series generalized to more dimensions.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: CMB anisotropies and angular power spectrum
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives readers a familiar handle on why the temperature pattern is decomposed into ℓ modes.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The expansion is on the two-dimensional sphere in spherical harmonics (the book calls it three-dimensional), and each ℓ corresponds to an angular, not a spatial, scale.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Sphere viewer where the learner adds individual ℓ modes and watches the sky pattern and its power spectrum build up.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The last scattering surface is every observer's own sphere, like the edge of visibility around a ship in fog (fog image is our addition).
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The book stresses that the surface is not a special place but depends on where and when the observer is.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In cosmology the 'fog' is in the past, not merely far away: we see the surface as it was at decoupling, and it recedes as the observer ages.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Two observers in a 2D expanding universe each see a different circle of last-scattering points; moving one observer moves its circle.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Wheeler's 'big U': the universe as a tube whose far end is the big bang and whose near end is an eye looking back at it.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Closing image for the idea that the universe produces observers who study its origin; also a nostalgic nod to Lieber's illustrated book.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Purely symbolic; it makes no testable claim and should not be read as a physical model.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The critical density is one fixed number valid for all cosmic time.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The density needed for flatness is 3H²/8π at each epoch and changes as H changes; the book attaches the name to today's value, and §26.7 uses the time-dependent ρcrit(t). Being near critical today says nothing directly about the density at other epochs.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is quoted as a single number, like a constant of nature.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A flat universe must have Ωm = 1.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: With a cosmological constant, flatness means Ωm + ΩΛ (+ Ωr) = 1; ΛCDM is flat with Ωm ≈ 0.3.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Older presentations without Λ equate flatness with Ω = 1, and §26.1 begins that way.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Closed universes always recollapse and open ones always expand forever.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Once Λ ≠ 0, geometry and fate are decided by different curves in Fig. 26.2; a closed model with enough Λ expands forever, and an open model with negative Λ recollapses.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: True for Λ = 0 dust models, which dominate introductory treatments.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The CMB comes from a special shell or edge of the universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Radiation was released everywhere at decoupling; the last scattering surface is simply the set of points whose light reaches a given observer now, and other observers see different spheres.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Diagrams show a sphere around us, and the word 'surface' suggests a physical boundary.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since the universe has cooled, the relic radiation should no longer have a thermal spectrum; a perfect black body today would be a coincidence.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Frequencies and temperature both scale as 1/R, so hν/k_BT is unchanged and the ν³ factor dilutes like 1/volume; a black body stays a black body at a lower temperature.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Changing temperature suggests changing spectral shape.
concepts: preservation of the black-body form under expansion

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Hydrogen recombines when the average photon energy drops below the ionization energy.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The average-energy estimate (≈50,000 K) is about ten times too high: photons in the high-energy tail, vastly outnumbering atoms, keep hydrogen ionized until about 3000 K.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Comparing typical energies is the usual first estimate.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Counting the mass in stars gives the matter density of the universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Stars give Ω ≈ 0.01, ordinary matter from nucleosynthesis ≈ 0.04, and total matter ≈ 0.3; most ordinary matter is dark gas and most matter is non-baryonic.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Light is what we see, and galaxies look like collections of stars.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Black holes formed by stellar collapse could be the non-baryonic dark matter.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They were made from baryons and so count against the nucleosynthesis bound; only black holes formed before nucleosynthesis (primordial ones) could evade it.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Black holes are dark and not made of 'ordinary' stuff once formed.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because Ωr ≈ 10⁻⁴, radiation can be ignored in cosmology at all times.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: ρr/ρm grows as 1/R̃ into the past; radiation dominated before R̃ ≈ 2×10⁻⁴, which sets the early expansion law and thermal history.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: §26.1 drops Ωr to draw the model plane.
concepts: scaling of densities with the scale factor

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Everything we observe must have been in causal contact because it all started together at the big bang.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In decelerating expansion the particle horizon at decoupling spans only about 2° of today's sky; the past light cones of opposite sky points never meet, so their equal temperatures are unexplained without inflation.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: 'Started at a point' suggests a shared origin and contact.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Inflation settles the questions of homogeneity and flatness completely.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It replaces them with questions about what the inflaton is and why its potential has the right shape; the authors present it as one plausible mechanism among others.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Inflation is often taught as an established part of the standard model.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The evidence for dark energy leaves no room for doubt.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Combined data strongly favour ΛCDM, but the authors note possible evolution of Type Ia supernova luminosities and the averaging problem for non-linear Einstein equations as grounds some cosmologists cite for caution.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The concordance numbers are quoted with confidence.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Solving Einstein's equations for a smoothed-out matter distribution gives the smoothed spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The equations are non-linear, so averaging the source and averaging the solution need not commute.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In linear theories such as Newtonian gravity or electrostatics they do commute.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The big bang singularity is only an artefact of perfect symmetry; real irregularities would turn it into a bounce.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The Hawking-Penrose singularity theorems show singularities arise generically, so there is good reason to think the real universe was singular in the past.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Symmetric collapse often focuses matter artificially; perturbing it seems likely to avoid the focus.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Hubble constant is constant in time.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: H(t) = Ṙ/R evolves; 'constant' means the same everywhere at a given cosmic time, and H0 denotes its present value.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The energy E in the particle analogy is the physical energy content of the universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: E = Ωc/2 is a combination of curvature and expansion rate that plays the role of energy in a mathematical analogy; it is not a conserved physical energy.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The equation looks identical to kinetic plus potential energy.
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor

thought_experiments.name: Tracing two antipodal CMB photons to their origins
thought_experiments.setup: Photons reaching us from opposite directions left points P and Q on the last scattering surface; follow the past light cones of P and Q back to the big bang in a decelerating universe.
thought_experiments.lesson: The cones never intersect, so no event could have influenced both, yet P and Q have the same temperature: the horizon problem.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Conformal diagram where the learner places P and Q at chosen sky separation and sees when their cones overlap, with an inflation toggle.

thought_experiments.name: Running the cosmic thermometer backwards
thought_experiments.setup: Shrink the universe step by step using T ∝ 1/R: a thousandth of today's size, then the first second, then 10⁻⁴ s.
thought_experiments.lesson: The universe passes 3000 K (atoms ionize), 10¹⁰ K at one second (nuclei break up) and ~10¹² K (nucleons dissolve into quarks), organizing cosmic history by energy thresholds.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Rewind slider with a thermometer and a particle inventory that changes at each threshold.

thought_experiments.name: Nudging the early density away from critical
thought_experiments.setup: Start the universe with density slightly off critical at equality or earlier and let it expand with R ∝ t^{2/3} or t^{1/2}.
thought_experiments.lesson: The deviation grows with time, so to be within tens of percent today the early universe needed extraordinary tuning; exponential expansion reverses the trend.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Log-log plot of |1 − Ω| versus t with a draggable initial offset and an optional inflation interval.

thought_experiments.name: Letting a closed universe bounce
thought_experiments.setup: Take Ωm + ΩΛ > 1 with a potential barrier higher than E and start the universe large and contracting.
thought_experiments.lesson: It halts at a turning point and re-expands without ever reaching R = 0: some FRW models have no big bang.
concepts: effective potential for the scale factor
thought_experiments.app_idea: Drop the bead on the right side of the barrier in the potential explorer.

thought_experiments.name: Retuning the constants of nature
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine altering fundamental constants such as the electron charge slightly and ask what kind of universe results.
thought_experiments.lesson: Most such universes could not support life, which is read either as design or as evidence for anthropic selection among many universes.

thought_experiments.name: Running a lumpy universe backwards
thought_experiments.setup: Trace an inhomogeneous universe back in time and ask whether growing irregularities might deflect matter and avoid the initial singularity.
thought_experiments.lesson: Intuition suggests a bounce, but the singularity theorems say singularities are generic; the exact-symmetry result is not an artefact.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Animation of focusing geodesics with random perturbations, showing that focusing still occurs.

historical_notes.event: Predicted a relic thermal radiation background from a hot early universe; the prediction was later found again independently by Zel'dovich and by Dicke in the 1960s.
historical_notes.significance: Shows the CMB was a theoretical consequence of the hot big bang before its discovery.

historical_notes.event: While Dicke's Princeton colleagues were building a detector (from 1964), Penzias and Wilson found the background with an antenna built for satellite microwave communication.
historical_notes.significance: Discovery of the CMB, the key evidence for the hot big bang over the steady-state theory.

historical_notes.event: Space missions WMAP (2001) and Planck (the book dates it 2018, when its final results appeared; launched 2009) measured the CMB with increasing precision.
historical_notes.significance: Precision CMB data turned cosmology into a parameter-measurement science.

historical_notes.event: Published the 2013 CMB temperature power spectrum reproduced as Fig. 26.4.
historical_notes.significance: The peak structure constrains geometry and content.

historical_notes.event: Supernova redshift-magnitude contours and balloon CMB constraints, reproduced from Liddle in Fig. 26.5, jointly pointed to Ωm ≈ 0.3, ΩΛ ≈ 0.7 (late 1990s results; not dated in the book).
historical_notes.significance: Established cosmic acceleration and the concordance model.

historical_notes.event: The steady-state theory predicted a background spectrum with much more high-frequency energy than a black body.
historical_notes.significance: The observed black-body CMB favours the hot big bang.

historical_notes.event: Gave exact formulae for the dividing curves in the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane, which the book cites but does not reproduce.
historical_notes.significance: Source for the boundary curves drawn in Fig. 26.2.

historical_notes.event: Singularity theorems showing singularities are generic, invoked for the big bang.
historical_notes.significance: Supports a genuinely singular origin despite local irregularities.

historical_notes.event: Hawking's popular account (1988) is the basis of the book's anthropic discussion; Barrow and Tipler (1986) gave the technical treatment.
historical_notes.significance: Frames the weak/strong anthropic distinction used in §26.8.

historical_notes.event: The authors remark that Einstein, whatever his view of a personal God, held deeply that the universe could not have been made otherwise.
historical_notes.significance: Illustrates the design reading of fine-tuning; historians debate how to characterize Einstein's religious views.

historical_notes.event: The book closes its anthropic discussion with Wheeler's 'big U' drawing, likened to Hugh Lieber's surreal illustrations in Lillian Lieber's relativity book that inspired d'Inverno (Chapter 1).
historical_notes.significance: Brings the book full circle to its opening story.

historical_notes.event: Conformal cyclic cosmology mentioned as an alternative to inflation.
historical_notes.significance: Signals that the early-universe paradigm is not settled.

applications_and_observations.details: Inserting H0 into 3H0²/8πG gives a density equivalent to a few hydrogen atoms per cubic metre, similar in order to the actual mean density.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: ρcrit ~ 10⁻²⁶ kg m⁻³ (H0 = 100); 9.7×10⁻²⁷ kg m⁻³ for H0 = 72 (my evaluation)

applications_and_observations.details: Distance-ladder determinations with Cepheids and Type Ia supernovae; the book gives 72 ± 8 km/s/Mpc. Modern determinations disagree at the several-percent level (CMB-inferred ≈ 67-68 versus local ladder ≈ 73), a live 'Hubble tension' not discussed in the book.
Table of rough distances from the Sun to the edge of the visible universe; 1 pc = 3.08×10¹⁶ m ≈ 3.26 ly; nearest large cluster ≈ 20 Mpc.
The background is an almost perfect black body; after removing local effects its temperature varies by less than one part in 10⁴ across the sky, strong support for large-scale isotropy.
Black-body energy density at T0 converted to a fraction of critical density; neutrinos and gravitons add little.

applications_and_observations.topic: Decoupling and the redshift of CMB photons
applications_and_observations.details: Crude estimate 50,000 K, realistic 3000 K when the universe was 1/1000 of its present size; typical frequency then 1.6×10¹⁴ Hz, now 160 GHz; last scattering surface radius of order 6000 Mpc in the book (the comoving distance in ΛCDM is closer to 14,000 Mpc, my evaluation).

applications_and_observations.topic: Luminous matter and hot cluster gas
applications_and_observations.details: Stellar mass averaged over large volumes gives a small fraction of critical density; hot intracluster gas seen in X-rays shows extra baryons.
Nucleosynthesis predictions for hydrogen, deuterium, helium and lithium match observations only for a particular baryon density.
Orbital speeds stay roughly constant far beyond the visible disk instead of falling as r^{−1/2}, implying massive dark halos.
Standard-candle brightness versus redshift for distant supernovae compared with the exact d_L(z) of each (Ωm, ΩΛ) gives an elongated confidence region favouring ΩΛ > 0 and acceleration.
Acoustic peak structure in D_ℓ versus ℓ constrains geometry and content; first peak near ℓ ≈ 220 (about 1°).
Supernova and CMB strips intersect roughly perpendicularly; structure formation and bulk flows independently require Ωm > 0.2.

applications_and_observations.topic: Age of the universe in ΛCDM
applications_and_observations.details: Flat age formula with concordance values gives about 14 billion years in the book, compatible with ages of old stars; without Λ the age would be uncomfortably short.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: H0t0 = 0.964 → 13.1 Gyr for H0 = 72 (my evaluation); Einstein-de Sitter 2/3 → 9.1 Gyr

applications_and_observations.details: Gravitational lensing surveys towards the Large Magellanic Cloud detected some compact halo objects but too few to be all the dark matter.
Direct-detection experiments and accelerator searches for WIMPs have produced no conclusive signal; neutrino mass limits disfavour hot dark matter; axions remain undetected.
Zero-point energy estimates from the standard model exceed the observed dark energy density enormously.
Scaling estimates of key epochs with Ωr = 7×10⁻⁵, Ωm = 0.3, H0 = 72; equality temperature quoted as 30,000 K though R̃_eq gives ≈14,000 K.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: R̃_eq ≈ 2×10⁻⁴; t_eq ≈ 10¹² s ≈ 35,000 yr; t_dec ≈ 10¹³ s ≈ 350,000 yr; T(1 s) ≈ 1.5×10¹⁰ K ≈ 1 MeV; quark-hadron ≈ 2×10¹² K at 10⁻⁴ s; t0 = 4×10¹⁷ s; inflation as early as 10⁻³⁴ s

applications_and_observations.details: Extrapolating today's bound on |1 − Ω| back in time, and the angular size of causally connected CMB patches.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: |1 − Ω| < 10⁻⁵ at t_eq (book; ≈5×10⁻⁵ by direct scaling, my evaluation); causal patches ≈ 2° (≈1.2° in a ΛCDM calculation, my evaluation)

applications_and_observations.details: Computer simulations of gravitational instability reproduce observed galaxy clustering, but only with dark matter included.
Gravitational-wave detections combined with radio, optical and X-ray observations; the planned space interferometer LISA may detect signals from the early universe.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Signature (+, −, −, −) with G = c = 1, so the Friedmann equation carries 8πρ/3; SI factors (G, c, ħ, k_B) are restored for numerical work and in the exercises.
Ω = ρ(t0)/ρcrit; Ωr, Ωm, ΩΛ for components; Ωc = −k/(H0²R0²) for curvature (positive for open). All are present-day values.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Ωc corresponds to Ω_k elsewhere. ΩΛ is occasionally printed as Ω_λ. Ω also denotes the integration region in (26.64).

notation_and_conventions.convention: R̃ = R/R(t0), t̃ = H0t, t_H = 1/H0; R0 = R(t0). In (26.47) the symbol R stands for the normalized R̃.
notation_and_conventions.notes: H̃ in §26.7 is unrelated: it is the constant inflationary Hubble rate (the OCR copy renders it with a hat).
V(φ) in §26.7 is the inflaton potential, a different object.
In §26.3 h also denotes Planck's constant; the text warns about the clash.

notation_and_conventions.convention: k ∈ {−1, 0, +1} is the curvature index; k_B is Boltzmann's constant.

notation_and_conventions.notes: In §26.5 α also denotes the late-time exponential rate H0√ΩΛ.

notation_and_conventions.convention: d_L = r1R(t0) with redshift factors removed (Chapter 24 definition); r1 = sin χ, χ, sinh χ.
Distances in pc and Mpc; 1 pc = 3.08×10¹⁶ m ≈ 3.26 ly; H0 in km/s per Mpc.
In (26.55) T is in kelvin and t in seconds.

notation_and_conventions.item: Scalar field action and stress tensor

difficulty.notes: Section 26.1 needs only ODE separation, calculus on a potential and some algebra (the cubic step is skipped); §26.7's scalar-field part needs the book's variational machinery. The conceptual load is high because the chapter moves quickly across observational astronomy, statistical physics, particle physics and philosophy, with many results quoted rather than derived. Printed slips (the R̃ argument in (26.21)-(26.22), the black-body peak condition, 'Ωm = 0.7' in the age, the t_dec coefficient, T_eq, the exponent in (26.62) and the 8π in (26.71)) and inconsistent epoch numbers can trip careful readers. Observational values are dated relative to current precision cosmology.

teaching_gems.gem: Turn the Friedmann equation into a unit mass rolling in V(R̃) with energy Ωc/2, then read geometry-independent fates (big bang, crunch, bounce, eternal expansion) off the potential plot.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces algebraic case analysis with a mechanics picture every physics student already trusts, and the same picture later explains Hubble friction for the inflaton.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Potential explorer with Ω sliders, draggable bead start point and a live R̃(t̃) history.

teaching_gems.gem: Build the (Ωm, ΩΛ) map from theory first, then drop observational confidence regions onto the same axes.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners see exactly which qualitative question each observation answers and why two probes with perpendicular degeneracies beat one precise probe.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Universe atlas where synthetic SN and CMB data generate contours that the learner can tighten or rotate.

teaching_gems.gem: Derive the acceleration line in three lines: q0 = Ωm/2 − ΩΛ.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A compact, memorable result that makes 'dark energy causes acceleration' quantitative and shows matter counts half.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Tug-of-war graphic whose rope position is q0 as Ωm and ΩΛ sliders change.

teaching_gems.gem: Show why an old black body stays a black body: ν and T both scale as 1/R, so ν/T is invariant and ν³ tracks 1/volume.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Resolves a natural worry in two sentences and explains the spectacular thermal CMB spectrum.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Spectrum plot with an expansion slider that stretches the frequency axis and rescales amplitude, overlaid on a fresh black body at T/a.

teaching_gems.gem: Estimate decoupling from mean photon energy, get 50,000 K, then name the two reasons it is ten times too high.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Models good physical reasoning: a quick estimate, a diagnosis of failure, and the corrected physics (tails and photon-to-baryon ratio).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Counter of ionizing photons per hydrogen atom versus temperature for adjustable photon-to-baryon ratio, marking where it falls to about one.

teaching_gems.gem: A cosmic calendar from two scaling laws: T ∝ 1/R plus R ∝ t^{2/3} or t^{1/2}, anchored by T0, t0 and R̃_eq.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners can reproduce the whole thermal history with a calculator and see which assumptions matter.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Log-time slider with temperature, energy and dominant-component readouts, comparing the piecewise estimate with full numerical integration.

teaching_gems.gem: One horizon integral, two answers: Δr = 2t for radiation versus (e^{Ht} − 1)/H for inflation; one flatness formula, two trends: t^{2/3} versus e^{−2Ht}.

teaching_gems.app_idea: Toggle between power-law and exponential R(t) and watch both the horizon plot and the |1 − Ω| plot flip behaviour.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: (26.21), (26.22) and Exercise 26.6 write the rescaled solution as R̃(t̃/H0); since t̃ = H0t the argument should be H0t.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers checking dimensions get confused about whether time is multiplied or divided by H0.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present R(t) = R0R̃(H0t) and have learners verify R(t0) = R0 at t̃0 = H0t0.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The argument that E ≥ 0 excludes turning points relies on V < 0, which holds only for ΩΛ ≥ 0; with ΩΛ < 0 the potential becomes positive at large R̃ and all models recollapse. The recollapse boundary for Ωm < 1 is therefore ΩΛ = 0, not the cubic root.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may apply the rule to negative-Λ models and misread the lower part of Fig. 26.2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the ΩΛ ≥ 0 assumption explicitly and show a negative-Λ potential in the explorer.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The left panel of Fig. 26.1 is drawn with E = 0, although the text cites it for the E < 0 case with V_max < E.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Mild mismatch between figure and text.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label the parameter values used for each panel (my reconstruction: roughly (0.3, 0.7) and (2, 0.02)).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The cubic (26.28) is obtained 'after a bit of algebra', and cubing introduces extra branches; the physical roots are identified only by reference to Fig. 26.2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot reproduce the boundary curves or know which root to keep.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Solve (26.27) numerically in the app, or show the parametric solution, and discard roots that fail the uncubed equation.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The printed stationarity condition for the Planck spectrum is wrong (it should be 3(e^x − 1) = xe^x, i.e. x ≈ 2.82); the peak and mean energies are quoted as 2.7 and 3 k_BT rather than 2.82 and 2.70.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Anyone solving the printed equation finds no positive root.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Give the corrected equation and emphasize that the peak location depends on whether one plots per frequency or per wavelength.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text says most of the remaining chapter is Level 2, but the hatched bar covers only the black-body and decoupling part of §26.3.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Unclear which material a first-time reader may skip.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Mark in the app which parts need physics outside GR and provide short primers (black body, nucleosynthesis, scalar fields).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: §26.5 says to take 'Ωm = 0.7' in (26.30); the stated age of about 14 Gyr requires Ωm = 0.3 (ΩΛ = 0.7). With H0 = 72 the formula gives 13.1 Gyr; Ωm = 0.7 would give 10.2 Gyr.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A learner doing the calculation obtains an age that contradicts the text.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use Ωm = 0.3 and have learners compute both numbers to see the effect of Λ on age.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: §26.5 equates 10¹³ s with about 10⁶ years (it is about 3×10⁵ years), and says the matter-plus-Λ solution holds from just after decoupling; radiation actually stops mattering dynamically after equality, while the photons stop interacting at decoupling. Fig. 26.6 labels the atomic era at 500,000 years, the text 350,000.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Inconsistent epoch numbers undermine trust in the estimates.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Adopt one consistent set (t_eq ≈ 5×10⁴ yr, t_dec ≈ 3.8×10⁵ yr in modern ΛCDM) and flag book values as rough.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: (26.52) is printed with a missing coefficient ('≃ ×10¹³ s'); the scaling actually gives 1.3×10¹³ s ≈ 4×10⁵ yr. The matter-era law is also applied all the way from today, ignoring the Λ era.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot reproduce the quoted number exactly and may not realize it is order-of-magnitude.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the arithmetic t = t0(T0/T)^{3/2} and compare with numerical integration including Λ and radiation.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: T_eq is quoted as ≈10⁴T0 ≈ 30,000 K, but R̃_eq ≈ 2×10⁻⁴ gives ≈5000T0 ≈ 14,000 K.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Inconsistency between two adjacent results.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Recompute T_eq from R̃_eq and note that the (26.55) coefficient is consistent with an independent radiation-era calculation (Exercise 26.9).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In the first line of the χ derivation the integrand appears as dR/(R̃(r)R); it should be dR/(ṘR).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Obscures the change of variables.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Display dt = dR/Ṙ explicitly before rescaling.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The book's d_L lacks the (1+z) factor of the standard luminosity distance, so (26.46) differs from formulas in Liddle, Hartle and data papers.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners comparing with other sources or fitting real supernova magnitudes will be off by (1+z).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State both conventions and use the standard d_L = (1+z)R0S_k(χ) when working with data.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 26.4's caption links the peaks to dark energy, baryons and dark matter 'respectively', and the text calls the multipole expansion a three-dimensional Fourier series.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Oversimplified: the first peak's position mainly measures spatial curvature (total density); peak height ratios measure baryon and matter densities; the expansion is in spherical harmonics on the 2-sphere.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Explain acoustic oscillations qualitatively and demonstrate with a toy peak model and a sphere harmonic viewer.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The flatness extrapolation claims |1 − Ω| < 10⁻⁵ at equality; scaling 0.3 by (t_eq/t0)^{2/3} gives about 5×10⁻⁵, and the radiation-era law (∝ t) is not given for going earlier.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Numbers do not reproduce and learners miss that the growth rate differs by era.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show |1 − Ω| ∝ t in the radiation era and give the full piecewise extrapolation (e.g. ≲10⁻¹⁶ at nucleosynthesis).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: (26.62) shows [−e^{H̃u}/H̃] as the antiderivative; it should be [−e^{−H̃u}/H̃].
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A sign slip in an otherwise simple integral.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Rewrite the integral step explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: (26.71) gives H̃ = (V/3)^{1/2}, treating V like Λ; with the book's own (26.5) and H² = 8πρ/3 the rate is (8πV/3)^{1/2}.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners combining formulas from §26.1 and §26.7 get factors of 8π wrong.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Derive H² = (8π/3)(½φ̇² + V) from (26.69) and take the slow-roll limit.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Inflation is treated without the number of e-folds needed (~60), the shrinking comoving Hubble radius picture, the mechanism of reheating, or why the 2° horizon angle arises; Fig. 26.7 is a sketch rather than a true (conformal) spacetime diagram.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: 'The horizon grows exponentially' can be misread as a physical speed-of-light violation, and the argument's quantitative core is missing.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use a conformal diagram and the comoving Hubble radius 1/(aH) to show causal contact before inflation; compute the required e-folds.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The parsec is described using the width of Earth's orbit subtending one arcsecond; the definition uses the orbital radius (1 AU).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Factor-of-two confusion in the basic distance unit.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define the parsec via 1 AU and a parallax angle of one arcsecond.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Observational values are dated: H0 = 72 ± 8 (now a precise but disputed 67-73 'Hubble tension'), Ω_baryon ≈ 0.04 (now 0.049), and 'the Plank satellite in 2018' (Planck launched 2009, final release 2018). Recent large-scale-structure surveys have also reported hints that dark energy may evolve.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may quote outdated numbers or miss current debates.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present book values as a snapshot and add a live panel of current parameter estimates with uncertainties.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The last scattering surface radius is given as about 6000 Mpc without saying which distance measure; the present comoving (proper) distance in ΛCDM is about 14,000 Mpc, the light-travel distance about 4000 Mpc.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Conflicting numbers across sources confuse learners.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Always name the distance measure and show several on one diagram.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The anthropic section's example refers to a big bang about ten billion years ago, inconsistent with the 14 Gyr age given earlier; its strong principle is a multiverse version that differs from Barrow and Tipler's; and the claim about Einstein's beliefs is contestable.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may treat a philosophical, Hawking-derived framing as standard terminology.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present multiple formulations with attribution and keep the philosophical material clearly separated from physics.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 26.7 is keyed to §26.3 and describes the flat model as 'open'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor confusion when locating the relevant material.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Key it to §26.1 and say 'flat, with matter and Λ'.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If you knew only what the universe contains today and how fast it is expanding, could you tell its whole past and future?' Then introduce Ω's as the answer's language.
Before the formalism, make sure the learner recalls ρm ∝ R⁻³, ρr ∝ R⁻⁴ and ρΛ constant, and can explain each physically (dilution, plus redshift, plus no dilution).
Teach the sum rule by evaluating the dimensionless equation at today; ask: 'Why is dR̃/dt̃ equal to 1 now?' (Because Ṙ/R = H0 and R̃ = 1.)
Use the particle-in-a-potential picture actively: have the learner predict the fate for given Ω's by sketching V and E before showing the computed R̃(t̃).
Check understanding with q0 = Ωm/2 − ΩΛ: ask for the minimum ΩΛ for acceleration if Ωm = 0.3 (0.15) and whether a flat universe can decelerate (yes, if ΩΛ < 1/3).
Stress that geometry and fate decouple when Λ ≠ 0; ask for a closed universe that expands forever.
When discussing the CMB, separate three claims: it is thermal, it is isotropic, and it is cold because of expansion; ask which observation supports each.
Walk through the decoupling estimate as a lesson in estimation: let the learner compute 14 eV/3k_B, then ask what could make it wrong before revealing the tail and photon-number arguments.
For dark matter, sequence the evidence: stars (0.01) < baryons (0.04) < matter (0.3); ask what each gap implies.
Use the SN/CMB crossing picture to teach degeneracy: ask why a single probe gives a strip rather than a point.
Flag book errata when learners reach them: R̃(H0t) not R̃(t̃/H0); age uses Ωm = 0.3; peak condition 3(e^x − 1) = xe^x; H̃² = 8πV/3; exponent sign in (26.62); d_L convention.

For the flatness and horizon problems, derive both from the formulas already known and only then introduce inflation by changing R(t); ask the learner to predict what exponential expansion does to each formula.

Common learner question: 'Does inflation break the speed of light?' Answer: no local signal outruns light; the comoving region in causal contact before inflation simply becomes larger than today's observable universe.
Common learner question: 'Is dark energy the same as the cosmological constant?' Explain the geometric versus source-side readings, quintessence, and the vacuum-energy mismatch.
Treat the anthropic section as a discussion prompt rather than physics; ask what observation could ever distinguish the weak from the strong form.
Quote modern parameter values alongside the book's (H0 ≈ 67-73 with the tension, Ωb ≈ 0.049, Ωm ≈ 0.31, ΩΛ ≈ 0.69, T0 = 2.7255 K) and explain they are snapshots.
Close by linking back: horizons and singularities from black holes (Part D), gravitational waves (Part E) as future cosmological probes, and Hawking-Ellis as the next text.
